courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Why Culture Matters
courses.description:
This course is an introduction to culture, with an aim to broaden students' understanding of humanities in general as well as the relevance of culture to contemporary society. The course explores the relationships among cultural appreciation, cultural representation, cultural continuity and cultural criticism; it also examines how related knowledge and practices in the humanities are valuable of enriching, on the one hand, students' own value system and lifestyle, and, on the other hand, the overall betterment of society, particularly in the digital age of globalization. The course is not theory-based, but its purpose is to expose the students to the diverse strains of cultural thought and practice that are relevant to contemporary society, particularly that of Hong Kong, China and Asia. Relevant contemporary issues will be drawn extensively to explain the values of the humanities and the need for knowledge of cultural studies in the societies of Hong Kong, China and Asia.

The course covers four sections to explain the breadth of knowledge that can be applied to understand how culture works. The four sections include (1) basic introduction of cultural studies as an interdisciplinary field, (2) media representation in popular culture, (3) memory, history and modernity and (4) community, urban culture and critical pedagogy. The four sections show the trajectory of applying a cultural studies point of view to understand why culture matters in today’s fast changing world. The Chinese and English sections of the course will select from a total of 22 sub-themes to discuss the role of culture to art, technology, education and humanities.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Students will understand that culture is important in the building of a better society.

• They will also gain the ability in critically analyzing the diversity of values and interests in society.

• Students will be able to draw on a number of disciplinary origins within areas of the arts, humanities, and social sciences to appreciate the richness and the usefulness of interdisciplinary approach.

• Students will gain a critical respect for local histories, traditions, and appreciate the value of culture in humanities.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Public Humanities

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 402

courses.description: This course introduces students to the basic concepts and practices of public humanities, an emerging field that examines the influence of the humanities in the public sphere. It guides students through the ways in which humanistic thinking and inquiry can impact community engagement, collective cultural history and memory, policy-making, and the cultivation of empathy. Organized into three sections—Visions, Paths, and Experiments—each part focusing on different dimensions of public humanities, the course begins by exploring the conceptual foundations of public humanism, emphasizing the importance of curiosity, generosity, and collaboration. As the course progresses, students engage with real-world case studies that demonstrate how humanities initiatives can reshape culture and society. Students will also experiment with designing a small-scale collaborative project, which allows them to transform their public concerns and humanistic inquiries into concrete outcomes. These projects serve as a starting point for their further development within and beyond the programs of public humanities. The course is designed for students interested in leveraging the humanities to enrich public culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:*

1. *Analyze and Develop Public Humanities Projects:*

* Evaluate and curate small-scale public humanities projects, understanding their impact on community engagement and public scholarship.*

2. *Communicate Scholarly Research Effectively:*

* Utilize digital platforms to articulate complex ideas in a clear, accessible manner, effectively reaching and engaging diverse audiences.*

3. *Collaborate Effectively in Diverse Teams:*

* Work collaboratively to integrate diverse perspectives, assess team dynamics critically, and manage project challenges efficiently.*

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Research Methods in Public Humanities
courses.description:
This course offers an overview of research methods in Public Humanities, and equips students with the essential research skills, cultural sensitivity, and critical perspectives required to navigate this dynamic landscape. Through an immersive exploratory journey on research methods, students will engage in pilot research for a collaborative hands-on project, embodying the driving ethos of this course: engagement, praxis, and reflexivity. In this endeavor, students will explore diverse qualitative and digital research methods for investigating, documenting, and sharing stories, histories, and other forms of cultural mediation for community engagement.
This course is designed to foster an interactive and dialogic learning environment that cultivates peer collaboration and exchanges of insights. Building on the conceptual foundations laid in CURE1004 Introduction to Public Humanities, this course provides students with the practical skillset needed to unlock the transformative and empowering potential of humanities-based research that nurtures and nourishes the community.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Text and Image: a Critical Analysis
courses.description: This course is aimed at the students beginning their encounter with theory, in which they will learn the fundamental components of cultural criticism in terms of textuality and contextuality. Here the " text" is broadly defined as cultural artifacts, which includes filmic image, literary and historical narratives, social and everyday life experiences as well as media representation. The course materials are selected to give the students the basic information and guide to understand the object, the purpose and the method for cultural criticism. Topics discussed include intertextuality, defamiliarization, dramatic monologue, metaphor and montage, narratives and space-time structure, psychoanalysis and stream of consciousness, reader-response criticism and genre studies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
\* Textual and image analysis

\* Inter-cultural & multi-media sensitivity

\* Trans-disciplinary approach & critical skill

\* Critical and creative thinking through integration of theories and practices

\* Literacy in different forms of visual, verbal & textual expressions, understanding how meanings & affects are constructed in different media forms & genre

\* Cultural appreciation and cultural criticism

\* Communicative and presentation skills

\* Independent and contextualized research skills

\* Board-minded but strong in critical evaluation

courses.description: Despite their long history, the influence of many great religions can still be recognized in our contemporary world. This course is designed to introduce students to this influence of religion in various aspects of our modern life. It will explore a variety of religious themes such as religious myth, symbol and practice, as well as current religious issues in ethics and politics. In order to illustrate the religious presence in our contemporary life, we shall examine these themes by looking at cases of films, activities and practices that can be easily seen in the world today. It is an introductory course and expects no prerequisite knowledge from students.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes

1. To become familiar with the basic themes of the field of religious studies

2. To develop an understanding of the key religious issues in the contemporary world

3. To be able to reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition in the contemporary world

4. To be able to engage in analysis of religious phenomena, taking into account of the key themes and issues involved.

Attitude outcomes

1. To develop a critical yet sympathetic attitude in understanding religious phenomena.

2. To develop a sensitivity to religious dimension of human life.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: The Study of Religion
courses.description: This course introduces the various approaches (such as philosophical, sociological, anthropological, psychological) to the study of religion, and attempts to show how, by utilizing the fruits and methods of these approaches, the history of religions can become the discipline which has religion itself as a proper object of study. This course then focuses on the study of the chief elements of religious beliefs and practices. These will include the phenomenon of religious experiences, myths, symbols, rituals, prayer and beliefs.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes

1. To become familiar with the basic vocabulary of the field of religious studies

2. To develop an understanding of the theories of religion

3. To develop an understanding of the key issues in the study of religion

4. To be able to reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition

5. To be able to engage in a critical analysis of religious phenomena by the key approaches, taking into account of the key issues involved.

Attitude outcomes

1. To develop a critical yet sympathetic attitude in understanding religious phenomena.

2. To develop a sensitivity to religious dimension of human life.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chinese Culture and Its Religion
courses.description:
(UGEA1450 is double-coded with CURE1122.)

The aim of this course is to help students understand the basic religious characteristics of Chinese culture and the relationship between religions and the daily life of Chinese people. It also helps students to appreciate the richness and diversity of the Chinese traditions and acquiring essential preparation for more advanced courses in the area of Chinese culture and religions. The course is divided under the familiar categories of Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, and Popular religion. These traditions are, by no means, discrete and mutually exclusive. It will be demonstrated that they overlap and interact with each other through a variety of confluences and conflicts. Students will also be introduced to some primary source of the Chinese traditions including both textual and fieldwork data.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGEC1450 or UGEA1450
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) understand the basic religious characteristics of Chinese Culture

(2) appreciate the diversity of Chinese Culture

(3) able to have a comprehensive understanding of the essential characteristics of Chinese civilization through a cross-disciplinary approach

(4) learn to appreciate and evaluate, by way of an integrated approach, their own cultural heritage from a broad. historical, social and intellectual perspective.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: World Religions
courses.description:
(UGED1400 is double-coded with CURE1123.)

This course provides an introduction to some major religious traditions in the world from a phenomenological and historical point of view. Topics include Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Daoism and Local religions etc.. Through the study of religion in different cultures, this course seeks to broaden students' horizons and widen their academic experience.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGED1400.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:

(1) Students will be able to understand world religions in their historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally, locally and in their many facets

* (2) Students will be able to engage in a* critical analysis of religions by the methods of the humanities and social sciences

Skill Outcomes

(1) Students will be able to develop their skills associated with data gathering and direct observation; organizing it, understanding it, and presenting it.

(2) Students will be able to develop their skills in cross-cultural understanding and intercultural literacy.

Attitude Outcomes

(1) Students will be able to develop their ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious traditions especially those one does not belong

(2) Students will be able to develop their sensitivity to ultimate concern and religious dimension of human life

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Study of Christianity
courses.description:
(UGED1520 is double-coded with CURE1124.)

The primary aim of this course is to provide students a broad and comprehensive understanding of the Christian faith through introducing its characteristics, traditions, history, scripture, theology and ethics. It helps students to analyse critically the various forms of Christianity and appreciate the richness of the Christian religion that exerts so great influences on human civilizations. Through interdisciplinary dialogues, this course also aims at helping students to see how the Christian faith understands and deals with problems, predicaments, political and ethical dilemmas of humanity.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge:

* To achieve proper understanding of Christianity as a global phenomenon and some of the representative manifestations of Christianity in various local contexts.
* To obtain a comprehensive knowledge of the major aspects of Christian faith, especially its views of the meaning of human life.
* To have a basic understanding of the methodology involved in the multidisciplinary study of Christianity.

Skills:

* To be able to use the analytical framework and hermeneutical tools for the academic studies of the religious phenomena related to Christianity.
* To be capable of relating what have been leant from this course to some other academic disciplines.
* To have the ability to reflect critically on one’s own cultural and / or religious tradition.

Attitudes:

* To treasure the value of human life and be sensitive to the related ethical responsibilities.
* To appreciate the diversity within particular cultural and / religious tradition.
* To become more respectful to others’ religions, worldviews and values.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Interpretation of Art
courses.description: Targeting at students with no prior knowledge of art history, this course introduces students to methodologies and theories currently used by art historians and curators to analyze and interpret works of art. The course covers a range of themes such as representation, expression, form, style, Formalism, Iconography, Marxism, Gender etc. Using modern and contemporary Chinese art as examples, the course will equip students with transferable and analytic skills, knowledge of modern and contemporary Chinese art, aesthetic sensibility, and theoretical literacy, encouraging them to apply these methods and knowledge to the study of visual art.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Demonstrate knowledge of the basic approaches and methodologies in art appreciation
2. Understand of key issues of the visual arts in modern and contemporary China
3. Demonstrate facility in research skills and familiarity with primary and secondary sources
4. Demonstrate the ability to analyse critically works of art by adopting appropriate theories and methodologies

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Cultural Management
courses.description: Cultural management is frequently perceived as a new terrain both for the acknowledgement of the role of culture in driving economic and social development, and for the dissemination of managerial thought to arrange and plan cultural entities, facilities and services. This course first aims to facilitate students’ understanding of the rising discipline of cultural management, which is embedded in the transformative understanding of culture and the on-going global movement that highlights culture-led development. Second, it introduces the managerial approach to cultural assets, initiates students’ understanding of the relationship between arts management and the market system and government policies, and imparts the preliminary knowledge for the management of the arts. Third, it displays a spectrum of major issues in cultural management, such as cultural policy, cultural organizations and institutions, venue management and event programming, heritage, conservation and cultural tourism and cultural creative industries. The breadth of the discipline as indicated allows students’exposure to the basic cultural management concepts and strategies.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge enrichment, students are expected to achieve the understanding of the discipline of cultural management, including its objectives and values, its relationships with the transformative understanding of culture, the on-going global movement that celebrates culture-led development. Other major issues will also be covered. Students are expected to understand preliminarily the operation of art businesses and cultural organizations in connection to market values and government administrative systems. In terms of management training, students will learn practicalities such as cultural managerial principles, planning strategies and basic skills, issues, challenges and limitations specifically for the arts and cultural resources. Discussions are largely based in the local context, supplemented with overseas and Chinese cases, with an awareness of the variances across contexts.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Cultural Policy and Development
courses.description: The course is an introduction to the nature, functions and making of cultural policies. Making references to examples of local and international cultural polices, it studies the relationship between the making of cultural policy and the infrastructure of power, the ideological influences behind the making of cultural policy. It also studies the latest trends in cultural development and its relationship with policy-making, and the impacts on the development of arts and culture, with particular references to the local context. The course also includes a practical aspect of drafting and developing institutional policy as part of the studies in cultural management.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to learn about how cultural policy is composed, its scope and structure, and the ideological components behind it within the context of the infrastructure of power, and to understand the impact of cultural policy in shaping the development of culture. The course also intends to equip students with the skills of drafting institutional cultural policy, which is essential for the development of a cultural institution.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Cultural Studies
courses.description: Through examining texts, artistic forms and discursive practices that reflect and produce different cultures, students will take part in delineating the working definition(s), methodology and critical awareness of the subject. Concepts such as multiculturalism, diaspora, hybridity, globalism/localism, transnationalism will be discussed. Emphasis will be given to Hong Kong culture as a basic reference point in its contact and interaction with other cultures.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1) Knowledge Outcomes
Basic concepts in Cultural Studies
Historical developments of Cultural Studies in England and its expansion since the 1990s
Critical dimensions of the concept of culture and their relevance to everyday life cultural practices, the working of cultural production and consumption

2) Skill Outcomes
Independent academic research on new concepts
Analytical writing on cultural concepts and approaches of cultural criticism
Presenting ideas through reading and cultural analysis

3) Attitude Outcomes
Proactive in learning and research

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Cultural Studies of Space
courses.description: This course will examine the subject of space from the cultural studies perspective. The objective is to understand how space as a cultural phenomenon relates to matters of ideology, social class, nationality, ethnicity and sexuality. The course will investigate the ways in which meaning about space is generated, disseminated and produced through various practices, beliefs and institutions, and how understanding of space is embedded in the political, economic, or social structures within a given culture. Examples of space making and manifestation will be taken from both Hong Kong and overseas.
courses.learning_outcomes:
In terms of knowledge acquisition, students are expected to understand how space is defined and constructed and their impacts on the development of society in terms of the make-up of our regional, national and global orders; their role in the shaping of cultural practices, expressions and ideology; their relations to production and enterprising and hence their role in the shaping of our identity, taste and values as well as economy and policies. In terms of values and skills, students are expected to develop critical ability in analyzing the diversity of values and interests, inter-cultural sensitivity, a balance view of local and global issues, literacy in understanding different visual and textual meanings and forms and the ability to appreciate the importance and significance of the inter-disciplinary nature of space studies.

知識探索方面，預期同學可瞭解空間如何界定與構建，並明瞭其：對地區、國族、全球的秩序組成等社會發展的影響；在文化習性、表達、意識形態形塑中的角色；與生產及企業的關係，從而瞭解其在身分、品味、價值以至經濟及政策形塑中的角色。價值與技巧方面，預期同學可發展出分析不同價值及興趣的批判能力、文化互動中的敏感度、本地及全球議題的平衡視角、明瞭不同視覺及文本意義暨形式的理解力、領會空間研究的科際性質的重要性及含義之能力。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Culture and Travel
courses.description: There are two characteristics in culture: regional (space) and accumulative (time), and is the way to acquire various cultural experiences from different space and time. From the cultural perspective, there are different levels of travel: from "tourism" for pleasure, "travel" for different purposes, like study, works, business or military, to "journey" for life experience and eternal truth. This course aims to provide theoretical reflections and historical analysis on the relation between culture and travel, and in particular, the wide range of symbolisms of cultural experience of travel. It will be able to help students explore the process of crosscultural interactions as well as the knowledge of cross-cultural management in travel.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students should gain a much more critical and reflective understanding of travel experience and its power implications to both the hosts and the guests.
2. Students should be able to survey major social cultural theories on travels.
3. Students shall get to learn travel that is culturally innovative and socially responsible through the course’s fieldtrips.
4. Students shall learn to become a historically reflective and culturally sensitive traveler or responsible citizen when they travel around the world.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Film and Screen Studies
courses.description: This course focuses on the language and the basic theories of film/media. From formal, historical and theoretical approaches, students will learn how to analyze and critique the meaning behind the cinematic images; also, will learn to integrate one’s cinematic experience in terms of emotion and reason, and to develop one’s ability in film criticism writing. In the course of teaching, three aspects will be highlighted including the critical, functional and practical ones.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

- identify, describe, and analyze the technical aspects of film as art.

- deeply analyze in diverse ways of critical thinking on film/media, such as the views of genre, auteurship, and spectatorship, and grasp the ways to utilize these different analytical frameworks for the writing of film criticism.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Celebrity, Stardom, and Hong Kong Popular Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2245 is double-coded with CURE2007.)
Celebrity culture is generally understood as a cult full of short-lived trends and inconsequential fan behaviour. We seldom consider, however, the powerful influence it has over our cultural identities. This course examines how the interplay between celebrity culture and the cultural industry shapes cultural identity with case studies from Hong Kong as the major scope of study. Starting with a brief history of Hong Kong celebrity culture from the 1980s to the present day, the course offers an entry point for students to understand the intricate relationship between the media and celebrity culture, encompassing a wide range of cultural icons and phenomena such as action film actors, cross-media megastars, and YouTube micro-celebrities. Each case study will engage with key concepts in celebrity culture, such as star-text, commodification, authenticity, extratextual reading, and participatory reading. The course proceeds by introducing the critical perspective of cultural studies in making sense of representation politics, public culture, fandom studies, and the diverse modes of intimacy in the digital age. Overall, students will gain an understanding of celebrity culture and how identities are thus produced, promoted, and commodified in the wider arena of media and popular culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the subject, students will be able to:

* **Define and explain** the connotation of celebrity culture, stardom, and popular culture in contemporary society, and the genealogy of discourses development of Hong Kong popular culture over time.
* **Understand** on how cultural identities are shaped by the interplay between celebrity culture and the popular culture industry.
* **Employ** a selected range of methods to study the development and formation of celebrity culture and infer the meaning of such process in the Hong Kong context.
* **Reflect** on the impact of celebrity culture on the formation of cultural identities.
* **Demonstrate** the intersectionality of celebrity culture and the formation of cultural identities locally and globally.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Being Human in the Age of AI: An Introduction to Digital Ethics
courses.description:
(UGED2329 is double-coded with CURE2008.)
Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science are reshaping every aspect of contemporary life—from how we work and communicate to how decisions are made about health, education, and governance. This course introduces the ethical, social, and philosophical issues that arise from these technologies. Students will examine topics such as algorithmic bias, data surveillance, automation, misinformation, and AI’s impact on human agency and creativity. Drawing on philosophical frameworks, scientific research, and real-world case studies, the course encourages students to think critically about how technological systems embody values and power structures, and how they can be governed responsibly. The course aims to develop students’ ethical reasoning, cross-disciplinary understanding, and ability to articulate informed positions on emerging technologies. Through a team-based learning approach, students engage in weekly readings, discussions, and collaborative writing exercises that cultivate both independent judgment and cooperative problem-solving. No technical background is required.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Students should be able to:**

1. Analyze and Apply Ethical Frameworks: Identify and apply key ethical theories (e.g., virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) to evaluate the design and deployment of AI and data-driven technologies.
2. Evaluate Global Societal Impacts: Critically assess the social and political implications of algorithmic systems—such as bias, surveillance, and data colonialism—integrating diverse global and cross-cultural perspectives.
3. Construct Ethical Arguments: Formulate and defend informed, persuasive positions on the responsible governance and ethical use of emerging technologies in contemporary society.
4. Collaborate and Communicate Effectively: Work productively in teams to synthesize complex ethical ideas and communicate them clearly through collaborative writing and oral presentations.
5. Practice Critical Reflexivity: Reflect on one’s own assumptions, values, and agency as a user, designer, or citizen within an AI-mediated world.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Understanding Digital Humanities
courses.description: This course introduces students to theories and practices of digital humanities. The aim is to explore the technological shaping of human cultures through practices. Students will learn about the history, the rationale, the benefits, and the challenges of digital humanities. Each week, the lecture will introduce the historical trajectory of the fields’ development, its new configurations with the emergent technologies (such as Natural Language Processing and Language models). From week three onwards, each lecture will also include a short section focused on introducing a DH tool. Tutorials are dedicated times for students to put theories to work and to experiment with the DH tool of the week. By the end, students will have the skills to create, analyze, and critique digital humanities projects. Students will also learn to critique the field's practices and contributions. This course will explore the intersection of technology and culture and discover how students can shape the future of humanities research.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* **Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:***

* **Understand the fundamentals of computation and explain its possible connections to humanistic inquires***

* **Engage critically with debates about quantitative methods and data visualizations in humanities in both verbal and written form***

* Develop basic competence in using tools of DH through tutorial discussions and project demonstrations.*

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Disability Studies in Public Humanities
courses.description:
This course aims to build students’ foundational understanding of Disability Studies from the perspective of Public Humanities, and to explore how it transforms critical frameworks within the arts and humanities. It will guide students to analyze representations of disability in artistic and cultural texts, revealing their political, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions, and to consider “bodily difference” as a key category for cultural critique and social justice.
Students will compare theoretical discussions of different disability models within the humanities and social sciences, developing an understanding of the multiple meanings of “disability” as both a cultural and political concept. The course also emphasizes cultivating students’ critical reading and academic writing skills—including art criticism and cultural curation—while fostering inclusive pedagogy and principles of universal design.
Balancing theory and practice, the course covers themes such as disability and design, performance art, technological development, and global biopolitics. It encourages students to reflect on how modern societies define “normalcy,” “ability,” and “humanity.” Ultimately, the course seeks to equip students with a cross-cultural and interdisciplinary vision to understand and promote the public engagement and social transformation of inclusive culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:**

1. Demonstrate a foundational understanding of various approaches of Critical Disability Studies, including its key concepts, theoretical frameworks, and its transformative impact on Art and humanities and cultural critique.

2. Analyze Critically evaluate representations of disability in artistic, literary, and cultural texts, uncovering their political, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions.

3. Understanding “disability” as a cultural, political, and interdisciplinary concept.

4. Reflect on and critique societal constructs of normalcy, ability, and humanity, analyzing how these intersect with issues of race, gender, sexuality, and class.

5. Apply critical reading, academic writing, art criticism, and cultural curation skills, while integrating inclusive pedagogical practices and principles from CDS.

6. Engage with cutting edge theories in CDS such as Crip Theory, Biopolitics, and Design Justice to explore the intersections of disability with technology, performance, and global politics.

7. Formulate strategies to foster public engagement and social transformation through inclusive culture and accessibility, balancing theory and practice.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Body Politics and Representations
courses.description: This course explores issues related to the representations of the human body in various cultural forms, including literature, cinema, drama, photography, advertisings, and medical discourses etc. We critically interrogate and examine the logic and implications of these representations through close textual and contextual studies. With the help of contemporary cultural theories, we engage in theoretical discussions about the complex issues related to the body, covering topics of identity, society, gender, and sexuality. The aim of the subject is to help students to understand the cultural myths and the rich meanings of the human body, so that we can most intimately examine the formation of our identity and value system.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to understand how our cultural and social orders are made up of and maintained by representations of and various forms of discipline on human bodies. Students should be able to critically understand the many interests invested on the body, and critically evaluate the meanings of such diversity of values. With close studies of literary, film, and art texts, students are expected to develop literacy in visual and literary expressions. Reading theoretical texts from different disciplines, students are also expected to appreciate the richness and the usefulness of interdisciplinary approach

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Meaning in Motion: Dance, Theater and Culture
courses.description:
Dance is historically entwined with many cultures around the world. Dance has certainly played a significant role of ceremony, rituals, celebrations and entertainment since before the birth of the earliest human civilizations.

This course provides an understanding of the history, evolution, and universality of dance as an art form. Further, viewing dance as a social and cultural practice, the course aims at analyzing dance semantics and meanings in gestures, the interrelationship of dance and space, theatrical design and costumes, the formation of a dance to its social background, customs, as well as concepts of the self representation and embodiment in their dancing. In particular, students will have opportunities to experience learning the gestures encoded symbolic meanings with narratives of dances. To demonstrate a physical understanding of a variety of dance forms, this course allows them to explore the pleasure of creative process of choreography in workshops.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Articulate the role of dance in social, cultural and historical contexts.
- Lean the knowledge for interpreting the differences among world dances, rituals and traditions.
- Decode world dance semantics & cultural symbol
- Understand the interrelationship between dance, space and theater
- Comprehend the social meanings embedded in choreography, aesthetic valuing in dance and theater arts.
- Learn folk dance movement and be able to convey messages through body language.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Modernity and Urban Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2042 is double-coded with CURE2016.)

This course is an introduction to the formation of modernity in relation to various aspects of urban culture. Tracing the development of cities and the urban cultures evolved within the new urban development since the 19th Century, cities such as Paris, London, New York will serve as 'texts' for analysis. Architecture, urban planning, artistic and intellectual movements as well as modes of everyday life in urban living are studied to demonstrate how the modern ways of thinking, seeing and living come into being. The course will also focus on the specificity of Hong Kong's experience in urban development and its adaptation of 'modernity' during a process of urbanization. The course will employ a wide range of visual images and audio-visual materials to explain the dynamism between modernity and urban culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
To equip students with basic theories and concepts of urban studies, modernity, cultural geography, and critical theory.

To equip students with critical skills in analyzing the dynamism between modernity and urban culture in relation to examples from various visual and literary genres.

To enable students to use interdisciplinary critical perspectives to probe different dimensions in the phenomena of urban culture

To provide strategies to articulate cultural theories with our practices of everyday life

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Living in the Anthropocene: Nature, Culture and Power
courses.description:
(UGEC2243 is double-coded with CURE2018.)

Human have altered the environment in ways that have no precedence in human history. Ecological crisis, environmental degradation, and extreme weathers have become the watchwords of contemporary politics. The conventional boundaries between “nature” and “culture” are now being questioned. How do nature, culture and power intersect in our everyday life? How do we get to understand issues of sustainability and environmental crisis from a broad historical perspective and global activism angle? How are gender, class and race interact with technology, damaged environment, animal and plant species? This course explores these questions and the rich debates in the emerging field of environmental humanity and literature of the Anthropocene.

Class topics are organized on major global green movements that resisted oil pollution, toxic factories, logging companies, dam constructions and nuclear plant building. Students get to learn the historical developments of major environmental activism in the West and the global south. How was the Greenpeace founded? What is the Narmada Dam Movement in India? Do you know Ken Saro-Wiwa, an environmental activist against Shell oil pollution in Nigeria? In each class we examine historical texts, visual materials and theoretical debates to explore how environmental justice has been intertwined with histories of colonialism, neoliberalism, and questions of gender, race, poverty and class. Together the class explores the problem of the Anthropocene (Nature) in the context of colonial history, grass root struggles (Culture) and corporation greed (Power).

This course addresses many of the 17 United Nation Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Climate Actions (13), Life on Land (15), Life below Water (14), Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions (16), Clean Energy (7), Reduced Inequalities (10), and Gender Inequality (5). Students are able to identify the weekly course content aligned with specific SDGs and be able to understand these goals in both historical and contemporary contexts.
courses.course_attributes:
SDG-GE #5 Gender Equality
SDG-GE #7 Affordable and Clean Energy
SDG-GE #10 Reducing Inequality
SDG-GE #12 Responsible Consumption and Production
SDG-GE #13 Climate Action
SDG-GE #14 Life Below Water
SDG-GE #15 Life On Land
SDG-GE #16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* Acquire knowledge on major environmental struggles and movements in the West and the Global South
* Comprehend the historical relationships between ecological crisis, colonialism and corporate politics
* Analyze the current ecological crisis using the concept of slow violence
* Evaluate the scientific debates of the Anthropocene with knowledge and analysis from the field of environmental humanities.
* Acquire the awareness and contextual understandings of the United Station Sustainable Development Goals

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Power, Identity, and Inequality in Medicine
courses.description:
This course is an introduction to the medical humanities, an interdisciplinary field of study that seeks to understand the social context of health and illness beyond the hospital, clinic, and laboratory. In particular, this course will emphasize the historical and cultural shaping of health disparities and examine how issues of power contribute to unequal patterns of risk and disease in our modern society. To do this, students will learn major theories and methods in the cultural study of health and medicine to understand how culture, power, and identity—including race, gender, capitalism, and colonialism— shapes the management of disease and individual illness experience in both Asian and global contexts. A critical concern in this course is how the organization of medical care confronts questions of social justice in medical treatment and public health in historical and contemporary contexts. Students will also grapple with the question of whether our institutions of medicine and public health function as a form of social control. By introducing students to the social components of health and illness, it aims to foster cross-disciplinary conversations across the faculties of arts, medicine, and other divisions at CUHK.

Following the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal of Reducing Inequality (SDG #10), a central question in this course is how medical treatments, research, and public health confront, or fail to confront, issues of social justice in global contexts. Students will learn theoretical approaches to health and inequality to investigate how history, culture, and politics shape the illness experience of socially marginalized people. These theories will enable students to assess the strengths and limits of our current arrangements of medical care and approaches to global health. In addition, students will learn critical medical humanities methods, such as ethnography, and use these methods to propose solutions to our current shortcomings in health governance. This course will challenge students to imagine better alternatives to our unequal world and demonstrate why the study of culture matters in medicine, global health, and public policy.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Analyze how social inequality shapes disease outcomes (SDG #10)

- Explain how media shapes public understandings of health and disease, including stigma

- Situate individual illness experience in the social, political, and cultural contexts of disease

- Implement the use of ethnography to develop health policies that can reduce inequality (SDG #10)

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Feminisms: Thoughts and Movements
courses.description:
(UGEC2273 is double-coded with CURE2022.)

A long-lasting struggle of gender equity was triggered by the women’s movements in England and U.S in the end of 19th century. Feminists fight for equality by publications, demonstrations and organizations. In 20th century, the feminist movement matured. Feminists have been more sensitive to the differences among women of different race, class, culture, religion and circumstances and noticed the importance of differences in unity. This course will introduce the strategies and main arguments of various kinds of feminism. Through learning from others’ experience, history and our daily life, we will understand the development of diversity in feminisms. We can have more understanding of feminists fighting for the right of disadvantage groups by self-review and mutual criticism in different times and culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. 解釋女權運動的歷史脈胳

2. 比較女權主義各種流派的生成與時代變遷之關係

3. 分析近代與現今性別權益事件

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Taiwan New Cinema and Beyond: Authorship, Transnationality, Historiography
courses.description: This course aims to familiarise students with the key works of the Taiwan New Cinema movement and its legacy beyond Taiwan and into the twenty-first century. It will explore not just the work of a wide array of film directors, but also the texts and the condition of their production, distribution, exhibition and consumption within a transnational framework, all of which impinge on the question of “national” film historiography. It will examine, in particular: the socio-political background of the emergence of the Taiwan New Cinema movement, its key directors and their works, the international context of their reception and the transnational nature of their production, and its legacy to date. It will provide students with an in-depth knowledge of the work of selected film authors and an awareness of the cinematic, cultural, and socio-political contexts in which they work, and enable students to analyse the work in relation to questions of transnationality and historiography.
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of this module, you should be able to:

Module-specific skills:

a.Demonstrate an advanced appreciation of the historical development of the Taiwan New Cinema movement, and its key directors and films.

b.Demonstrate an informed appreciation of how concepts of film authorship can be related to modes of production, modes of funding, and an international context of cinephilia.

c.Demonstrate an advanced critical understanding of key debates on the various aspects of transnational cinemas, from production and distribution to the analysis of texts and authors.

d.Demonstrate an advanced critical capacity to interrogate the notion of “national cinema” and the way in which it has been challenged in film historiography.

Discipline-specific skills:

a.Demonstrate an advanced capacity to analyse films from different periods in the Taiwan New Cinema movement and to relate their concerns and modes of expression to their historical contexts.

b.Demonstrate advanced analytical skills in the close formal, thematic, generic and authorial analysis of different kinds of films.

c.Demonstrate advanced intellectual and critical skills in the research and evaluation of relevant material for the study of film and communicate these conclusions effectively and fluently using appropriate critical and technical language.

d.Demonstrate an advanced capacity to consider the relationship between film and its complex production conditions and to relate film history to a wider context beyond the national.

Personal and key skills:

a.Undertake independent research on the basis of a taught course.

b.Adopt a critical approach to the selection and organisation of a large body of material in order to produce, to a deadline, a written, oral or visually sustained argument of some complexity.

c.Present a cogent and sustained argument orally / in writing, in English, on an aspect of the subject of the student’s own choosing, and selecting appropriate methods of exposition.

d.Using bibliographical material provided, select, plan and carry out a programme of study leading to an essay / presentation on a chosen topic, to a specified length and deadline.

e.Demonstrate ability to combine a variety of IT skills in researching and reporting on a topic.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Contemporary Consumer Culture
courses.description: This course surveys a wide range of topics on the commercialization of sports, tourism/leisure as an encounter of cultures/citizens/space, shopping mall and public sphere, and the impact on social and cultural life by the phenomenon of McDisneyization. Other topics such as advertising and pop culture, broadcasting (narrowcasting on the Net), merchandising and iconography in fashion will be examined to review key contemporary issues and debates about cultural consumption. Bringing together work on reception theory in literary studies and philosophy, studies on consumer culture in anthropology and sociology and those on media audiences within media studies, we will address the consequences and effects of increasing cultural commodifiaction and globalization, by exploring into the complex interactions of cultural production and consumption which are relevant in topics such as place and identity, visual culture and hyperreality, representation and communication technologies. Films and animations will be viewed outside class time. Field trips may be arranged.
courses.learning_outcomes:
With this course we embark on a self-investigative journey into our dominant way of life—consumption. Here we are going to de-familiarize consumer society and our daily consumption practices, in order to learn how patterns of consumption work, and to consider consequences of such culture.

We approach the topics with a number of theoretical perspectives, arguments, and illustrations. Students are expected to look into these everyday occurrences with sociological, anthropological, literary, and philosophical analytical tools. This course may help us reflect not only on our relationship with commodity in general, but also our increasingly mediated connection to the world, our community, and even to ourselves. The mediation as such is not so much in the traditional, materialistic sense of use and pleasurable experience, as melting of all that is solid into signs and their consumption. Emphasis will be placed on developing students’ analytical as well as cultural critical skills, or in other words, ability to un-learn the born-again consumer.

1) Knowledge Outcomes
Theories and perspectives of contemporary consumption culture
Characteristics of consumer culture and their global nature
Consequences and ethical appropriation of consumerism

2) Skill Outcomes
Articulating theories and practices in understanding phenomena of consumption
Creative project making to address to some of the obvious problems in consumerism

3) Attitude Outcomes
Balance between critical and pedagogical approach
Creative learning and un-learning through everyday life experiences

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Photographic Culture and Visual Communication
courses.description:
Photographs have tremendous power to communicate information; on the other hand, encoding and decoding metaphors of photographs present a unique set of challenges. This course can help students interpret and understand photographs meaningfully, later they can learn how to convey messages creatively.

This course combines both the theoretical and hands-on approach to allow students to explore their creative visual expression and to learn the technical applications of the photographic medium such as camera basics, lighting and digital applications. It discusses the fundamentals of photography from the historical, cultural, aesthetical and technological perspectives.

In particular, this course will cover aesthetical theories, social reflections, various genres of photography. To ensure that students be successful in their own personal and educational goals, they will be asked to create a digital portfolio on the Internet, as well as making selected photographic assignments of presentable quality.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Analytical Ability: Learn to think critically about the surrounding world of
imagery, to show a deeper understanding of the way aesthetic knowledge and value judgments impact photographic art. Uses case studies to explain photographic practices in contemporary art and place them in the context of theory

2. Creative Explorations: to broaden the student’s horizon by making them knowledgeable about most influential photographs that changed the world; Develop and enhance his/her proficiency in the vocabulary of the photographers. Above allows students to develop an individualized creative style and gain informed insights.
3. Technological skills: Learn to convey messages through the lens, understand the primary controls of a camera, and develop problem-solving skills; to acquire a general understanding of digital imaging applications.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Hong Kong Cinema
courses.description:
(UGEC2241 is double-coded with CURE2030.)

This course is a survey of Hong Kong cinema, with emphasis on its contemporary development. This course will cover both textual and contextual analyses: we treat Hong Kong cinema as an art form and introduce different ways to appreciate them and criticize them; we also read these films as commercial cultural products to investigate links between movies and society at-large. The course will introduce basic film theories and film languages. It helps students to reflect on their own relationship with these Hong Kong movies they grow up with, as well as help elucidate the complex relationship between Hong Kong cinema and Hong Kong identity.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
CURE2030 is double-coded with UGEC2241.
Not for students who have taken UGEC2241 or 2774.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to acquire a general understanding of basic film languages, and to develop basic skill in film appreciation and film criticism. After the course students should be able to understand Hong Kong history and Hong Kong society from the perspective of cinema, with critical awareness of related issues pertaining to gender, class, and cultural identity. They are also expected to understand the intimate relationship between film production and film consumption, as well as the differences and connections between art and commerce in the domain of Hong Kong cinema.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Youth and Popular Culture
courses.description: This course studies the relationship between youth and popular culture, specifically in view of the rapidly expanding youth culture in recent years. We explore the importance of the factor of age in the study of popular culture, explaining why youths are vulnerable to the manipulation of popular culture, and why their lifestyles and values also dominate popular culture. We also examine how youth identity is constructed around the dynamics between mainstream identity and subcultural identity, and students are given the chance to analyse their own socio-cultural worlds in the various cultural environment, including home, school, concerts, shopping malls, youth magazines, and the cyber-space. This course provides students with an understanding of why youths, in particular, are prone to collective identity, and how they achieve their sense of self through fashion, music, sports, and entertainment.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Knowledge Outcomes
- Integration of theories and practices
- Cross cultural contexts, including local, regional, and global
- Cultural approach to the study of contemporary living
- Articulation of cultural discourses and the everyday life
- Cultural embedding of representation and the media
- Local, regional and global perspectives

2. Skills Outcomes (Generic and Discipline/Professional)
- Textual and con-textual analysis
- Cultural appreciation and cultural criticism
- Critical and creative thinking
- Visual literacy

3. Attitude Outcomes
- Aware of multicultural communities and respect for the other
- Being confident in expressing ones ideas
- Board-minded but strong in critical evaluation

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Queer Theory and Culture
courses.description: Queer Theories emerged in the 1990s as some of the most vital analytical tools in the fields of Gender Studies and Cultural Studies. This course offers students an opportunity to study this strand of critical thought in-depth. It will examine theories of queer from four major approaches, namely: historical, political, reading and performative. Topics of the course will cover a wide range of subjects including identities, sexualities, temporalities, homophobia, activism, deviance, and transgression. This course is particularly suited for students who would like to acquire the knowledge of a particular theoretical approach and to engage it in a critical examination of literature and culture today.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Cultural Policy
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the historical and contemporary debate in Hong Kong and around the world on what constitutes culture and how governments and other organizations can help sustain cultural development. Particular emphasis will be placed on the context of Hong Kong and other cosmopolitan cities to examine how cultural policy can help shape a pluralist society. We will also discuss the challenges and distortion posed by economic and management criteria practised in today's capitalist societies to the intrinsic value of culture and the arts.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge acquisition, students are expected to understand how policies on culture is shaped and their impacts on the development of society in terms of the make-up of our regional, national and global orders; their role in the shaping of cultural practices, expressions and ideology; their relations to production and enterprising and hence their role in the shaping of our identity, taste and values as well as economy and policies. In terms of values and skills, students are expected to develop critical ability in analyzing the diversity of values and interests, inter-cultural sensitivity, a balance view of local and global issues, literacy in understanding different visual and textual meanings and forms and the ability to appreciate the importance and significance of the inter-disciplinary nature of cultural policies.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Trans-Asian Bodies and Visual Fantasy Cultures
courses.description: This course analyses how Asian bodies and identities are represented in media and visual fantasy cultures such as Japanese animation, social networks, and performative subcultures. We explore how the extreme cultural and social diversity of the Asian region contributes to unique perspectives on bodies and identities. We are particularly interested in the studies of trans-Asian cultural flows, which includes not only commodities and entertainments but also migrations, like workers, and specific thoughts, like Maoism or human rights. We believe that a careful reading of these transnational flows would help us reconsider what Hong Kong culture and Chinese culture mean in contemporary bodies and indentity. We compare the cultural studies of local cultures with the discourses of trans-Asian studies and globalization, with the aim to demonstrate the possible ideological traps and strengths of taking Asia as an academic category for studying the body and culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of the course, you will be able to:

1. Understand the diversity and similarities of different Asian cultures and subcultures in constructing the body
2. Understand the unique position of Asia in current discourse on the body and identity.
3. Able to critically apply or interrogate Western based theories with specific Asian case studies
4. Able to understand the relationship between cultural representations and social conditions of the body
5. Gain a unique understanding of Hong Kong and China from the perspective of Asia

學習成果：

當你成功修畢本課程之後將會：
1瞭解不同的亞洲文化和次文化在建構身體上的多元性和相似性。
2瞭解亞洲在當代身體和身分論述中的獨特位置。
3能夠批判性地運用或整合西方理論與特定的亞洲案例研究。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Television Studies
courses.description: This course aims to introduce the major studies of television understood as a set of institutions, technologies and texts shaped by historical, cultural, political and economic forces. This course examines television’s historical evolution; its relationship to other media; its preferred genres; its models of televisual spectatorship and consumption; its politics of representation in regard to class, race, gender, and sexuality; and its economic modes of operation. Upon completion of this subject, students are expected to understand the content and form of television as well as its industrial, social, cultural, and technological ramifications.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Identify and analyze important concepts in television studies
2. Analyze and interpret television as a form of creative expression with regard to its multiple genres, means of delivery, and formal methods
3. Evaluate relevant aspects of television that not only reflect on society but also shape values and meanings
4. Articulate their understanding of television as a complex medium with industrial, social, cultural, and technological ramifications.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Gender and Theatre
courses.description: The course aims to introduce the perspectives in gendering theatre which is especially suitable for students who have interest in performing art and gender studies. We will discuss when theatre is constituted as a realistic reflection or fantastic world, what kinds of gender issues can be raised out? Any arguments that performers and audiences voice-out and act-out? What kinds of fantasy can be passed? Through analysing scripts and performances, we will focus on the cultural politics of artists and reader/audiences, so as to point out the relationship between gender politics and theatre.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. 文本分析方法
2. 性別研究視角
3. 認識戲場與社會議題的關係

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Xiqu and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2294 is double-coded with CURE2042.)

The course introduces the student a basic knowledge of Xiqu (Chinese Opera), including its artistic features as a performing art, and the characteristics of different kinds of local Xiqu, such as Beijing Opera, Kunqu, Shanghai Opera and Cantonese Opera. Based on the basic knowledge of the art-form, we will discuss the cultural issues reflecting in the plays and performances. Through the textual analysis of scripts and performances, students will be introduced different topics of Xiqu related to cultural studies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
一、學生對戲曲藝術和歷史的基本掌握

二、介紹當代重要戲曲研究成果

三、啟發同學思考戲曲藝術與當代文化的關係

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Performance Studies
courses.description: Performances are actions, and "Performance Studies" is defined as interdisciplinary studies of human actions ranging from ritual, theatre, dance, music, popular entertainments as well as everyday life practice. The aim of this course is to provide the students with a knowledge of and insight into the key concepts, the historical development, and the socio-cultural implications of performance both in international scene and local context. Not only do we study the archives, the manifestations, the theory and the practice of various performers, composers, choreographers, actors, art and stage directors from different periods and traditions, but we also focus on the interpretation and communication, the audience reception and spectatorship of the social mass. It is a course draws on a wide variety of disciplines including social sciences, semiotics, speech-act theory, psychoanalysis, gender and queer studies, with which we can investigate the stylistic features, the quality of theatricality, the technical change, the hybridity and the boundary-crossing of performance in our era.
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of the course, you will be able to:
1. Understand the diversity and similarities of different Asian cultures from a cultural studies perspective
2. Understand the unique position of Asia in the current globalization discourse
3. Able to critically apply or interrogate Western based theories with specific Asian situations
4. Able to understand the relationship between cultural productions and social conditions
5. Gain a unique understanding of Hong Kong and China from the perspective of Asia

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Understanding Comic Arts
courses.description:
(UGED2326 is double-coded with CURE2051.)

Nowadays comic strip has become one of the major forms of visual narratives in our culture. Both comics and film are visual arts originally developed within the period of late 19th century and early 20th century. Although film has long ago established its artistic legitimacy, comic art still struggle for recognition. However, as Will Eisner put it, comic strip is a “Sequential Art” and has its own unique aesthetic nature. This course tries to inquire the governing aesthetic principles of comics and investigate its unique method of expression. We will also try to delineate the special communication mode of comics and its relationship with different aspects of modern society and culture. Students will learn to appreciate comic art from different perspectives, and strengthen analytical skills for visual media.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Through the lectures, students will recognize the aesthetic nature of sequential art and locate the humanistic values and meanings of comic arts for modern society and culture.

2. Through tutorial discussions, student will apply the analytical skills and formal methods to interpret comic and visual texts.

3. Through mid-term assignment (research portfolio on the visual representation of comics), student will distinguish, compare, analyze and criticize different visual and multimedia sources.

4. Through final paper, student will prepare and manage to do an academic research on visual representation.

5. Student will aware, judge and appraise the practical values of the analytical skills and historical knowledge provided by this course after they complete the mid-term assignment and final paper.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Foundation of Visual Design
courses.description: This practical class consists of lectures, readings, hands-on visual projects, and workshops, in which two main software will be taught: Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Premiere. Students will examine visual experiences from the perspectives of creators and viewers and will learn how to design images, edit videos, and add primary visual effects for their projects. At the same time, the practical work with these tools will help us better understand how they are used in society - the modes of thinking and inquiry they enable, their strengths and weaknesses.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- This course covers the basics of visual effects and post-production; students can use the tools as a creative medium in the context of contemporary art.

- Apply essential skills and concepts in the development of critical and innovative design outcomes.

- A broad overview of state of the art in new media art, critical design, and media theory.

- Students will gain experiences from technologies and methods related to visual cultures

and aesthetic functions in learning design.

- Develop students’ aesthetic sensitivity and the ability of visual aesthetic judgment. - Enhance students’ portfolio for job seeking.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Myth, Symbol and Ritual
courses.description: This course deals with the inter-relationship of myth, symbol and ritual, which are believed to play important part in human religious configuration. The human meaning of myth, symbol and ritual will be recovered in the context of social, cultural and psychological effects upon their believers. Meanwhile, theories and historical examples will be emphasized.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to understand:
(1) the role of myth, symbol and ritual in the human religious configuration;
(2) the various theoretical approaches to the study of religions and their social, cultural and psychological effects upon their believers; and
(3) the way religious symbol, myth and ritual interact with society: how they operate within, and are produced by society.

Attitude outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students are expected:
(1) to understand how myth, symbol, and ritual operate, consciously or unconsciously, in our daily life;
(2) to develop a critical approach to examine the various components embodied in religious faiths;
(3) to be able to cross disciplinary boundaries with an analytical mind; and
(4) to be able to integrate theory and practice.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Philosophy of Religion
courses.description: This course is a study of the nature and significance of religious experience and phenomena in human life and culture, the meaning of religious languages and concepts, and the justification of religious knowledge, particularly beliefs about God and man, in relation to various theories of reality and truth.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Sociology of Religion
courses.description: An introduction to the scientific study of the social aspects of religion from the sociological point of view. This includes an exploration of the interaction between religion and culture; a survey of religion as a social institution; and an examination of the relationship between religion and other major social institutions.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes
1. To understand the sociological major definitions of religion
2. To understand the major methodologies and key issues of the sociological study of religion
3. To be able to analyze religious phenomena by using the sociological approach

Attitude outcomes
1. To develop a critical yet constructive attitude in understanding religious phenomena.
2. To develop a sensitivity to religious phenomena in modern societies.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Psychology of Religion
courses.description: An examination of various aspects of religion from a psychological perspective. The contribution of such men as W. James, C. Jung and A. Maslow will be considered.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completion of the course, students are able to:
1) demonstrate familiarity with the conceptual debates and controversies within the psychological study of religion.
2) identify key concepts in psychological studies of religious experiences and beliefs.
3) discuss how religion informs an individual's worldview and social behaviors.
4) apply important concepts, theories, and research findings from the course to study religious phenomena.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Hong Kong Taoism
courses.description: The aim of this course is to explore the historical development of Taoism as a religion in Hong Kong. It will examine the historical link between Hong Kong Taoism and Taoism in traditional China, and will show how the activities of Hong Kong Taoism reflect the local religious characteristics of Hong Kong people.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1、認識香港道教歷史傳統及源流

2、了解香港道教信仰及文化

3、認識道教的節誕和習俗

4、參訪道觀和道教儀式

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chinese Buddhist Classics

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
