courses.description: This course aims at developing students' ability to read a Chinese Buddhist text in depth. The first part of this course will be dedicated to a study of some recent models of textual studies in the field of Chinese Buddhism. The second part of this course will be devoted to an analysis of a text chosen from the Chinese Buddhist canon. The text will be studied critically through a historical analysis of the circumstances surrounding the creation and dissemination of the text. The choice of text will be based on the interest of the students but it will be chosen among some of the most representative traditions of Chinese Buddhism such as the Chan, the Tiantai, or the Huayen School of Buddhism.
courses.learning_outcomes: To be able to understand religion in its historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally and locally and to analyze how contemporary religious expressions shape and are shaped by global and local cultural, social, and political trends.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Christianity and Western Literature
courses.description: The purpose of this course is to expose students to the interactive relationship between Christianity and Western Literature. It may include literary works such as Augustine’s Confessions, Boethius’ Consolation of Philosophy, Abelard’s History of Calamities, Dante's Commedia, Shakespeare’s King Lear, Milton's Paradise Lost, Goethe’s Faust, Tolstoy’s The Kingdom of God is Within You, Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov, etc.; and focuses on the themes of creation, sin, fall, suffering, love, spirituality, redemption, purgatory, forgiveness, pride, peace, Kingdom of God, Nature, etc.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1) Knowledge: Students will gain basic understandings of the relationship between Christianity and Western Literature.

2) Skill: Students will learn the skills of interpreting literature from both literary and religious perspectives

3) Attitude: Students will acquire the attitude to respective different interpretations regarding literature as well as religion.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduct'n to Taoist Literature
courses.description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the Taoist literature in Chinese history. While there are many approaches to the understanding of the discipline of religion and literature, this course covers traditional Chinese literature in relation to Taoist thought, practice, institution, and symbolism. The focus is on the formation of literary genres as religious expression and transcendental imagination in the context, as much as possible, of the development of Taoist religion. This will allow us not only to realize literature as the principal record of Taoist tradition in its confirmation and valorization of Taoist values, but also to grapple with the literary challenge to inherited orthodoxies and thus the undermining of conventional ideas and feelings, as well as to sample the texture of literature functioning as an alternative or substitute for Taoism. In this way, we can approach the intersections of the aesthetic and the religious as the essential humanity through the reading and analysis of the Taoist dimensions of literature.
courses.learning_outcomes:
微觀：

1. 對中國歷史上的道教文學有基本的認識；
2. 明白中國傳統文學與道教教義、儀式、制度和象徵的關係；
3. 對歷代文學作家創作背後的道教宗教性語景有基本的認識；
4. 對道教表達信仰及想像的基本體裁；
5. 以宗教現象學的研究視野，通過文學明白道教的宇宙論、鬼神觀、身體觀、道德觀等基本概念在文學中的呈現；
6. 通過文學讓同學明白道教作為中國土生土長的宗教，在文化長河中的位置及影響力。

宏觀：

1. 學習從出土文物、藝術、文學及經典文獻等第一手了解宗教現象；
2. 掌握搜尋學術論文等第二手資料的能力；
3. 明白在了解一個宗教時，需要用不同的視野進行探索。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion and Ethics
courses.description: An examination of the relationship of the Christian and various other world views to ethical issues of contemporary society.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Life and Death in Religions
courses.description:
Life and death are the central concerns in most religious traditions, which are usually transmitted through religious texts and rituals. Related themes include body, good life and good death, meaning of life, etc.

This course will take a thematic approach to examine the issues related to life and death in major religions in the world, including the Chinese, Indian, and Abrahamic traditions. At the end of the course students should have gained a comprehensive understanding of the life-course models, the symbolism of death, the death rituals and the meaning of life in these major religious traditions.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: New Religious Movements
courses.description: This course is designed to provide students tools and concepts with which to understand and study New Religious Movements (NRMs) and to promote religious tolerance. This course is divided into three parts: first of all, the significance and the methodological issues of New Religious Movements; secondly, some important issues on New Religious Movements, including rituals, gender, and economic dimension; third, Theoretical consideration and critique.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Foundational Medieval Latin
courses.description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Latin grammar and reading skills. Students will master fundamental structures including: noun declensions and cases, regular verb conjugations, adjective agreement, pronouns, and basic syntax. The course develops essential vocabulary and translation skills through carefully selected Latin readings of progressive difficulty.
Through systematic study of grammar and syntax complemented by regular practice in translation, students will build the foundational competency needed for reading Latin texts. By the end of the course, students will be able to read adapted Latin passages, demonstrate command of basic grammatical structures, and be prepared for intermediate-level Latin study.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Master basic Latin pronunciation and demonstrate competency in reading aloud, with proper attention to syllable length and stress
2. Demonstrate competency in fundamental Latin grammar, including recognition and formation of basic noun and verb patterns, declensions, conjugations, and essential pronouns
3. Build and effectively use a basic Latin vocabulary focused on high-frequency words and common expressions, enabling comprehension of simple texts
4. Read, translate, and analyze adapted Latin texts with proper attention to basic grammatical structures, including cases, tenses, and word order

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Beginning Sanskrit
courses.description: Sanskrit is India's venerable and ancient language of learning, a key sustainer of 'high' culture and religion since at least 3000 years that continues today to be an important medium of religious, literary, and philosophical discourse. It is also of great importance in much Buddhist as well as Hindu texts, and factors importantly into several southeast Asian languages and cultures. This course will introduce the language, overviewing essential and intriguing features while providing basics in pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary to appreciate its richness and expressiveness.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge and attitude outcomes
At the end of the course, a student should be able to demonstrate:
1. knowledge and understanding of Devanagari letters and sandhis.
2. knowledge and understanding of basic Sanskrit grammar and vocabulary.
3. knowledge and understanding of the basic Sanskrit structures and expressions.
4. the ability to understand simple narrative texts in written Sanskrit on topics of Indian religions.
5. the capability and awareness of utilizing a classical language in religious studies.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion, Health and Healing
courses.description: Religious traditions contain particular understandings of body and mind, health and wholeness, illness and suffering, healing and transformation. This course will cover the latest discussion on the relationship among religion, health and healing. Also, it will explore the health/healing beliefs and practices in different religious traditions such as Taoism, Judaism, Christianity, Muslim, and New Age Movement, as well as will contrast those beliefs and practices with the hegemony of secular western biomedicine. The central goal of the course will bring students to understand how religious health/healing practices are constructed and experienced as meaningful in today's rapidly changing and globalized world.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completion of the course, students are able to:
1) understand the ways that body and mind, health and wholeness, illness and suffering, healing and transformation are constructed in different religious traditions such as Taoism, Judaism, Christianity, Muslim, and New Age Movement.
2) understand the roles that religious practices can play in developing therapeutic understanding and facilitating effective healing process.
3) critically compare the health/healing beliefs and practices in religious traditions and in western biomedicine systems.
4) understand the importance of a holistic approach to health and healing.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Intermediate Seminar
courses.description: This course bridges introductory material and senior seminar course. It aims to help students integrate knowledge and skills acquired in junior years and prepare themselves for senior study. It will review the major approaches to Religious Studies and examine examples of current scholarly research in the field. Students will learn techniques for planning, conducting, evaluating, and presenting research.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completion of the course, students are able to:

1. Describe and explain the theoretical framework in the field of Religious Studies.

2. Identify and contrast different theories employed in the field.

3. Apply theoretical understanding to case studies.

4. Synthesize and evaluate key concerns in the field.

5. Analyze and assess scholarly materials in Religious Studies.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topics in Religion and Culture
courses.description:
An opportunity for guided research and study of selected topics, such as: methodological approaches to the study of religion, theories of religion, folk religion, festivals, religion in transition in contemporary society, the Mother goddess, religion as salvation, ritual and sacrifice. The Special Topics will also be covering Religion and Culture, including:
- Religion and Culture in Mesopotamia
- Religion and Economic Life
- Religion and Film
- Religion and Gender Studies
- Religion and Pluralistic Culture
- Religion and Politics
- Religions, Violence and Peace
- Religious Education and Developmental Psychology
- Religious Fundamentalism and Asian Cultures
- Buddhist Art in Dunhuang
- Any other topics related to Religion and Culture

Students are allowed to take this course not more than twice, and gain the units each time they pass the course.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

Knowledge outcomes

a.    become familiar with the basic vocabulary of the field of religious studies

b.    develop an understanding of the key theories, concepts, and issues in the study of religion

c.    reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition

d.    engage in a critical analysis of religious phenomena from the perspectives of the key theories and concepts in religious studies.

Attitude outcomes

a.    develop a critical yet sympathetic attitude in understanding religious phenomena

b.    develop a sensitivity to the religious dimension of human and cultural life

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Buddhism
courses.description: Buddhism has demonstrated a visible ability to adapt to changing cultures and regions for over 2,500 years. This course provides students with a general introduction to Buddhism. In this course, participants will investigate various thematic and specific aspects concerning the long and complex histories of Buddhism. Through the use of primary and secondary literature, film, and other media, this course will provide a regional overview of the development of Buddhism from ancient India to contemporary Western society. While we will try to follow the chronological development of Buddhism since antiquity, the focus of this course is more concerned with addressing key components that have shaped many different culturally specific Buddhist practices and doctrines. Course participants will be exposed to many of the unique philosophical, doctrinal, practical nuances and distinctions resulting from these cultural adaptations.
courses.learning_outcomes:
This course will enable course participants to:

Knowledge Outcomes

(1)display adequate understanding of core Buddhist concepts and identify distinctions between various Buddhist practices, doctrines, and histories

(2)demonstrate critical reflections on the relation between Buddhist teachings and worldly values

Attitude Outcomes

(3)develop sensitivities and awareness of cross-cultural issues and begin to understand how they have shaped Buddhism into various modes of doctrines and practices

(4)nurture a larger sensitivity to the value of Buddhist practice in human life

Skill Outcomes

(5)develop improved writing skills to better articulate the data/questions/issues extracted from course readings and discussions;
(6)develop skills necessary for close textual readings and analysis of relevant materials.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion and Food
courses.description: This course explores the intersection of beliefs/worldviews, health, and dietary practices in various religious traditions. Students will examine how different religious beliefs and customs shape the relationship between food and health within these traditions. The course will provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of religious beliefs on dietary restrictions, rituals, and the overall well-being of individuals practicing these religions.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* Understand the beliefs and customs that influence food choices and restrictions in various religions.
* Understand the cultural and social aspects of food consumption within religious communities.
* Critically analyse the dietary practices of different religious traditions, including Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity, and Hinduism.
* Critically analyse the role of food in expressing faith and spirituality within religious communities.
* Evaluate the impact of religious dietary practices on health and well-being.
* Apply the concept of fasting as a religious practice and its effects on physical and mental health.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Religions
courses.description:
Are religion and sex always at odds? How can religious aspects such as symbols, myths, taboos, rituals, and practices help us understand body, healing, medicine, gender fluidity, and sexual practices?
Rather than simply dividing religions into different traditions, this course takes a thematic approach and examines religion, gender and sexuality as crucial systems of power that shape our world. Students will develop an understanding of religion and gender as both subjects and as categories of analysis. As categories of analysis, students will use gender and religion to interrogate cultural production and social systems, paying close attention to how gender and religion intersect with other categories of social difference. Students will connect the assigned academic readings to “real-life” examples in the news, media, and their own lives, thereby producing new theoretical understandings of gender, religion, and sexuality in the contexts of Hong Kong, Asia, and the world.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Identify key scholars in the field and their theories, both classic and emerging
2. Demonstrate in depth knowledge of religion and gender as intersectional categories of analysis
3. Actively reflect upon ordinary/accepted modes of thinking about gender, sexuality and religion, construct new modes of thinking oriented toward change
4. Demonstrate a critical, intersectional awareness of gender and religion in the social and cultural contexts of Hong Kong, Asia, and the world
5. Develop critical reading skills of academic literature on religion and gender, including reading, analysing, and summarising the argument of secondary literature; selecting and analysing primary materials including visual contents
6. Develop communication skills through class discussion and writing assignments
7. Develop research skills
8. Develop transferrable skills

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Intermediate Latin
courses.description:
This course builds upon foundational Latin skills to develop students' proficiency in reading and analyzing Latin texts. Assuming basic Latin competency, we will advance through increasingly complex grammatical structures, with particular emphasis on: Middle and passive voices, Infinitive constructions, Subjunctive clauses and their sequence, Participial phrases and ablative absolute, Gerunds and gerundives, Complex relative clauses, Indirect discourse, and Conditional sentences.
The course centers on intensive study of selected classical prose, primarily from Cicero and Seneca, supplemented by readings from other classical authors. These authors provide an excellent progression in syntactical complexity while offering varied prose styles. Through these readings, students will strengthen their command of advanced Latin grammar, expand their vocabulary, and develop sophisticated translation techniques. Special attention will be given to developing sight-reading skills and mastering complex syntactical structures. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to approach advanced Latin literature with greater confidence and analytical skill.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisites: CURE2154 or 2166 or 2167 or its equivalent
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Demonstrate mastery of advanced Latin grammar, including complex verbal systems and clause constructions
2. Apply comprehensive Latin vocabulary knowledge and understand word formation patterns and derivatives
3. Read and comprehend elementary to intermediate-level Latin prose from classical authors with proper attention to style
4. Analyze and translate unseen Latin texts of moderate difficulty with accurate grammatical explanation

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Latin for Law, Social Sciences and Humanities
courses.description:
Latin for Law, Social Sciences and Humanities introduces students to fundamental Latin language structures while focusing on terminology essential to social sciences, humanities, and legal studies. This course requires no prior knowledge of Latin and welcomes students from all academic backgrounds. While particularly relevant for those pursuing studies in law, social sciences, humanities, and related fields, the course provides all students with valuable insights into social, cultural, and legal concepts through the lens of Latin terminology.

The course is structured in two complementary components. The first develops core Latin language competency, covering essential grammar including noun declensions, verb conjugations, and basic syntax. The second component applies this linguistic foundation to specialized vocabulary and concepts across disciplines, including philosophical terminology, psychological concepts, legal principles, sociological terms, and historical discourse. Students will learn to analyze and construct complex terms through understanding Latin roots, prefixes, and suffixes common in humanities and social science discourse. By course completion, students will be able to comprehend and correctly use Latin-derived terminology in academic and professional contexts, while acquiring sufficient Latin language foundation to pursue intermediate Latin studies if desired.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Demonstrate basic understanding of Latin grammatical structures, including fundamental noun declensions, basic verb conjugations, and simple sentence patterns essential for analyzing academic and legal terms
2. Recognize and explain common Latin roots, prefixes, and suffixes frequently encountered in legal, social sciences, and humanities terminology
3. Correctly interpret basic Latin phrases and terminology commonly used in legal documents, philosophical texts, and academic discourse in social sciences and humanities
4. Apply basic Latin language skills to decipher unfamiliar academic and professional terms by breaking them down into their component parts
5. Connect fundamental Latin expressions to modern concepts in law, social sciences, and humanities, demonstrating awareness of how classical Latin influences contemporary academic and professional discourse

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Latin for Science and Medicine
courses.description:
Latin for Science and Medicine introduces students to fundamental Latin language structures while focusing on scientific and medical terminology. This course requires no prior knowledge of Latin and welcomes students from all academic backgrounds. While particularly relevant for those pursuing studies in sciences, healthcare, and related fields, the course provides all students with valuable insights into scientific and medical concepts through the lens of Latin terminology.
The course is structured in two complementary components. The first develops core Latin language competency, covering essential grammar including noun declensions, verb conjugations, and basic syntax. The second component applies this linguistic foundation to specialized vocabulary and concepts in scientific and medical fields, including biological taxonomy, anatomical terminology, pharmaceutical nomenclature, and scientific processes. Students will learn to analyze and construct complex technical terms through understanding Latin roots, prefixes, and suffixes common in scientific discourse. By course completion, students will be able to comprehend and correctly use Latin-derived terminology in scientific and medical contexts, while acquiring sufficient Latin language foundation to pursue intermediate Latin studies if desired.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Demonstrate basic understanding of Latin grammatical structures, including fundamental noun declensions, basic verb conjugations, and simple sentence patterns essential for analyzing scientific terms
2. Recognize and explain common Latin roots, prefixes, and suffixes frequently encountered in scientific and medical terminology
3. Correctly interpret basic Latin phrases and terminology commonly used in scientific classification, anatomical descriptions, and medical prescriptions
4. Apply basic Latin language skills to decipher unfamiliar scientific and medical terms by breaking them down into their component parts
5. Connect fundamental Latin expressions to modern scientific concepts, demonstrating awareness of how classical Latin influences contemporary scientific and medical discourse

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Reading Religious Classics

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713

courses.description: The classics of different religions offer a wealth of insight and wisdom about nature, reality and life. Reading important religious classics is an essential way to acquire an in-depth understanding of the crucial doctrines and philosophy of a religion. This course gives students a chance to critically read classics, in their original languages or in translation, from one to two of the following religious traditions: Daoism, Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism. The texts will be analyzed with a focus on their religious thoughts, and the traditions and skills of interpreting respective classics. Texts selected for reading may include Zhuangzi, The Heart Sutra, The Bible and The Quran, The Bhagavad Gītā, and religiously inspired literary classics such as The Divine Comedy and The Journey to the West. The exact choice of texts will be decided by the teacher who offers the course in a particular year.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course, students should:

1. be able to read, understand and analyse samples of religious classics, with an awareness of the underlying cultural, social and historical contexts.

2. have reached a good awareness of the textual study of a specific religious tradition, and be familiar with the main relevant resources.

3. have acquired the basic linguistic and methodological skills to undertake independent research on religious texts, working on primary sources.

4. have improved basic academic skills, including critical reading, research, writing, and discussion skills.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Classical Arabic for Beginners I
courses.description: With the study of designed texts and relevant passages from the Qur'an, this module introduces students to the fundamental grammar and syntax that both Classical and Modern Literary Arabic are commonly shared. Students are first introduced to the Arabic script, followed by the rudiments of Arabic grammar and syntax. To keep this course relevant and interesting, some Arabic phrases and dialogues in daily conversations will also be taught.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CURE2151 (Arabic Beginners I)
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon the completion of this course, students are expected to:

The course provides ample opportunities to make considerable development towards the comprehension of the Arabic language in general and Qur'anic Arabic in particular.

The graded introduction of Arabic grammar and syntax will intensify the understanding of the language and create confidence among students in a non-Arabic speaking environment.

Student's skills are developed towards the comprehension of unvocalized Arabic text and translation of unseen Arabic text.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Classical Arabic for Beginners II
courses.description: The course 'Classical Arabic for Beginners II ' is suitable for students who have studied CURE2151 Arabic for Beginners I or CURE2180 Classical Arabic for Begninners I. This course aims to continue the learning of grammar and syntax that both Classical and Modern Literary Arabic are shared through writing, reading, listening, conversation, and through the study of relevant passages from the Qur'an. The learning of Arabic grammar and sentence structure is also consolidated. By the end of the course, students are expected to have basic proficiency of the Classical Arabic language.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Pre-requisite: CURE2180 or ARAB1000
Not for students who have taken CURE2150 (Arabic Beginners II)

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Indian Religions
courses.description: India among its one-billion population arguably represents the world's greatest diversity in religious and cultural thought, practice, and expression. This course aims to bring students in touch with the major religious traditions and cultural patterns of India. It also aims to awaken appreciation and understanding of how diverse peoples of India negotiate their lives within this complex religious and cultural landscape. The main question and thematic thread running through the course will be how the various traditions understand, express, and practice embodiment and transcendence. In other words, what are the constituents, changes, relationships, and possibilities for human beings and divinities with reference to the temporal world and transcendent reality? Where can we find significant "family resemblances" – without ignoring differences – among the diversities of persons and sub-traditions within those roughly designated Hindu, Jain, Buddhist, Muslim, Sikh, or Christian?
courses.learning_outcomes:
As a way to understand important dimensions of religion in general this course aims to expose students to aspects of Indian ‘spirituality,’ or the varied ways people of India understand and pursue ‘higher purpose’ and ultimacy. Having seriously engaged with the course students can expect to have:

1) A basic acquaintance with religious ideas and practice in the Indian subcontinental context.

2) A basic ability to grasp the feel and logic of traditions of spirituality in India sympathetically yet critically.

3) A basic competence in reading, listening, speaking and writing about the topics treated in the course.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Islam
courses.description: This course aims to give students an understanding of Islam as a religion along with an insight into the crucial issues facing Muslims throughout the world today. The course introduces the beginnings of Islam by looking at pre-Islamic Mecca, the life of the prophet Muhammad, and the revelation of the Qur'an. The beliefs and practices of Muslims are explored through an indepth look at the five pillars of Islam. The variety of Islamic beliefs will be discussed in an investigation of Shi'i and Sufi traditions. The course concludes with contemporary issues of Islam in the world, interfaith connections, the place of women in Islam, and the presence of Muslims as political minorities in the West. In addition to this structure, local references to Islam in Hong Kong will be used to give an enhanced local perspective to these topics.
courses.learning_outcomes:
To be able to understand religion in its historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally and locally and to analyze how contemporary religious expressions shape and are shaped by global and local cultural, social, and political trends.

Ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious traditions especially those one does not belong.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Taoism
courses.description: This course aims at introducing Taoism as a Chinese religion embedded with ancient Chinese religious culture. Topics of the study will cover history of main Taoist sects, Taoist divinity, Taoist conceptions of immortality and life and death, Taoist ritual and Taoist canonization.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students should have the knowledge to:

- understand basic concepts in Taoist Studies

- understand the development of Taoism from the Han until contemporary period

- understand Taoism in Hong Kong today

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religious Traditions and Politics of the Arab World
courses.description: The "Arab World" today refers to a large geographical area: from the Atlantic coast of North Africa in the West to the border of Iran in the East. Arabic is the principal spoken language of this region, which is also linked by shared cultural and religious traditions. The course presents a historical survey of the "Arab World" from pre-Islamic times to the modern era. The first part of this survey the rise and spread of Arab political rule and Arab language and culture with the advent of Islam in the 7th century, with later emphasis on some of the principal political, economic, social, religious, and cultural developments and their relevance to the contemporary "Middle East" region. Two main themes referred to throughout the course will be the unity and diversity of the "Arab World" and how various Arab cultures and societies have interacted with other peoples in this region and beyond.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

Knowledge Outcomes

Understand religion in its historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living. Understand religion in its many facets.

Engage in a critical analysis of religions by the methods of the humanities and social sciences especially through historiographical studies. Recognize central themes and issues in the Arab World, especially with respect to cultural and religious dimensions.

Skills Outcomes

Communicate and present (orally and in writing).

Gather, organize, deploy, synthesize and evaluate different types of evidence and information.

Claim English proficiency in reading and writing with accurate referencing and clarity of expression. Demonstrate cross-cultural understanding and intercultural literacy.

Attitude Outcomes

Have awareness of plurality and multi-faceted complexity within Arab cultural, political and religious traditions, and of the issues of multiple and conflicting interpretations of language and symbols, texts and traditions.

Acknowledge the contested and provisional nature of knowledge and understanding. Show tolerance of diverse positions and have respect for others' views.

Have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious and cultural traditions, political viewpoints and ideological positions, especially those one does not belong.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chinese Temples and Festivals
courses.description:
(UGEC2500 is double-coded with CURE2375.)

This course is a study of Chinese temples and festivals. Temples are cultural heritages which preserve as mute testimony to local history. Their structures and the use of ornaments also reflect traditional architectural characteristics. "Jie dan" (festivals), including birthdays of the gods and jiao rituals, are the ritual activities being held for prosperity in folk culture. The belief system, indigenous custom, human diasporas as well as community cohesiveness of the Chinese can be illustrated from both temples and festivals in China and Hong Kong.
courses.learning_outcomes:
¨認識廟宇、節誕與民間文化的關係

¨通過廟宇、節誕實例，使同學了解香中國及港歷史與社會變遷

¨廟宇、節誕如何反映香港文物保育與文化遺產保存的工作

¨從廟宇看傳統建築與藝術雕飾的特色

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religions, Violence and Peace
courses.description: Conflict seems a natural activity of human beings. It commonly results from contrasting ideas, perceptions or limited resources. It widely appears in diverse issues such as family ties, social justice, political ideologies or environmental concerns. This course is designed to provide students a process of (1) analyzing the assumptions, sources, and types of interpersonal, inter-group, and international conflict with the ideas of race, ethnicity, religion, and culture; (2) studying various forms of non-violent conflict resolution, and (3) studying both the relationships between religion and peace building.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completion of the course, students are able to:

1. analyze the many facets of conflict and how conflict plays a role in human history and in our daily lives ;
2. discuss ideas about the value of conflict (e.g. that it can be constructive, relationship building, and necessary for growth and change);
3. study systematic means of conflict resolution and investigate alternatives of non-violent problem solving.
4. apply religious and moral values to issues of justice and peace.

完成此課程後，學生能夠：
1. 分析衝突的不同面相及其在人類歷史和日常生活中的角色；
2. 了解衝突的價值所在（如，衝突可以是建設性的、有利建立關係、或是發展及變遷所需的）；
3. 探索解決衝突的系統化途徑和非暴力的問題解決方法；
4. 運用宗教與倫理的價值到公義、和平等議題上。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Art Institutions in Twentieth-Century China
courses.description: The course examines the correlation between art and institutions in twentieth-century China, aiming to encourage students to think about modern Chinese art through the concept of the artworld. The downfall of the Qing dynasty and the establishment of the Republican China transformed the social and institutional organisation of the production, distribution, and consumption of art as well as the traditional patronage system in modern China. The structural changes conditioned the emergence of formal and informal art institutions that facilitated yet constrained artistic practices, laying the foundation for the development of a modern art world in China. The course looks at the history of modern Chinese art and the formation of different art institutions in the sociocultural and economic context of modern China. Weekly topics are structured chronologically and thematically, which cover a wide range of themes, including art schools, art societies, museums, exhibitions, and art market. Adopting an interdisciplinary approach, the course offers students multi-perspectives to understand the transformation of modern Chinese art and the interactions between artistic practices and society in modern China.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Explain the theory of the artworld and history of art institutions in modern China.

• Identify and describe the historical background, aesthetics, and social factors reflected in specific artworks.

• Identify and interpret the correlation between artistic styles and the institutional organisation.

• Reflect upon the roles of art institutions in the process of art creation, production, distribution and consumption.

• Select research materials and develop original research topics on modern Chinese art.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Heritage Management
courses.description:
Cultural heritage management presents a complex landscape influenced by globalization, urbanization, cultural place-making projects, technological advancements, economic development, and diverse applications in both the preservation of history and the creative industries. As cities expand and integrate globally, the challenge of preserving local cultural identities while balancing heritage conservation with modern urban needs becomes increasingly significant. In recent years, technological innovations and the development of smart cities have enhanced accessibility and supported cultural initiatives, transforming heritage preservation. However, issues of sustainability and resilience in dynamic urban environments worldwide have also emerged as critical topics and debates within cultural heritage management.
This course aims to provide students with an introductory knowledge of cultural heritage management, along with the theoretical frameworks that shape our understanding of cultural heritage. It covers policy at international, national, and local levels, conservation and restoration practices, funding and resource management, and ethical considerations. While highlighting the significance of intangible cultural heritage, this course will also examine the impact of tourism and the vital role of community involvement, intersecting with issues of identity, technology, urban planning, and conflict. By offering a variety of foundational concepts and real-world case studies, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of current practices and challenges in cultural heritage management.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT2004, UGED2285.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explore key historical and contemporary examples of cultural heritage projects, along with the theoretical frameworks that shape our understanding of cultural heritage.
* Understand cultural heritage policy at international, national, and local levels, with a focus on conservation and restoration practices, funding, and resource management.
* Examine critical issues related to the preservation, interpretation, and dissemination of heritage, including ethical considerations.
* Develop skills to critically analyze intangible heritage, assess the impact of tourism, and understand the vital role of community involvement.
* Reflect on broader issues concerning identity, technology, urban planning, and conflict as they relate to cultural heritage management.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing methods of preserving, interpreting, and disseminating heritage.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Management of Public and Non-profit Cultural Organization
courses.description: Public and non-profit cultural organizations are positioned in the core part of traditional arts management education. This course aims to equip students with knowledge on the characteristics of public and non-profit cultural organizations as one type of cultural organizations, and mastery of the key management components of public and non-profit cultural organizations, including strategic planning, structural design, human resource management, leadership building, financial planning and fiscal management, marketing cultural products, and the organizations’ internal and external control and performance evaluation. A series of in-class exercises and individual and group projects is designed to develop students’ knowledge and management skills simultaneously.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge, students are expected to gain an understanding of the specificities of public and non-profit cultural management, which are different from general management based on the understanding of the characteristics of those organizations and the profession. Students are also expected to achieve an overall picture of all the key components in non-profit cultural organization management. More emphasis, however, is placed on the students’ capacity to apply the knowledge of management to practice by enriching solid skills. Through this course, students can design the structure of a cultural organization, plan for strategies for organizational development, and enact internal and external controls. Their major final product will be a business plan for creating and managing a non-profit cultural organization. In addition, the students can acquire software technical training to develop portfolio design and job application skills.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Understanding Chinese Art through Exhibitions

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408

courses.description:
(UGED2286 is double-coded with CURE2406.)

The exhibition has become a site of knowledge production and a prominent and diverse part of contemporary culture. Regarding “Chinese art” as a social constructed concept, the course uses “exhibition” as an entry point to engage with issues concerning Chinese art and to explore the role played by exhibitions in the formation of the knowledge of Chinese art. It introduces the current theories and debates on the theory and history of exhibition, and the display methods, examining the changing concept of Chinese art and curatorial practices through detailed analysis of case studies. The first part of the course traces the formation of the concept of “Chinese art” by looking closely at the history of exhibitions on Chinese objects from the late Qing dynasty to the early twentieth century. The second part examines important exhibitions that have shaped our understanding of Chinese art. Structured thematically, the course discusses the curatorial concepts of selective significant international exhibitions on Chinese art, and investigate how scholarly research has been transformed into exhibitions which have shaped our understanding of Chinese art, constructed identity and been deployed for political ends.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon the completion of the course, students will be able to:

·Explain the theories of exhibition and the changing concepts of Chinese art

·Identify and describe the important exhibitions on Chinese art and prominent Chinese art objects.

·Identify and evaluate the curatorial ideas of important exhibitions on Chinese art.

·Select research materials and Chinese art objects to develop original research.

·Design and plan a virtual exhibition based on original research.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Curation in Arts and Culture
courses.description:
“Curating,” a word that was once only used in museums, now has applications in everything in our lives, ranging from radio station DJs to almost all types of social media content. The popularity of the word reflects the growing importance of assembling, managing and presenting data and collection, a process of gathering information that brings maximum value relevant to different audiences.

In this context, this course is designed to provide students with an opportunity to learn about both historical and contemporary examples of how culture is understood through exhibition design and curating. By covering various forms of curatorial traditions, disruptive ideas, and emergent digital practices in the ever-expanding field of curation, this course equips students with the ability to question what they take for granted and reflect on existing issues conducive to different cultures, values and beliefs. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically examine how knowledge is created inside and outside of art institutions and how curation could potentially become public knowledge.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing this course, students will be able to:

• Explain key historical and contemporary examples of exhibition design and curating, relating to a wider local and global context

• Examine critical issues concerning ways that different cultures, values and beliefs are represented through curation

• Develop skills to critically analyze how knowledge is created inside and outside art institutions

• Acquire personal and social competencies to transfer curating into knowledge sharing and act as an active agent in facilitating knowledge engagement

• Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions in the ever-expanding field of curation

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: AI in Creative Industries: Applied Creative Technologies
courses.description:
In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force reshaping creative industries worldwide. From film production studios using AI for visual effects and script development to advertising agencies leveraging generative tools for campaign creation, the integration of AI technologies is fundamentally altering how creative professionals work, collaborate, and innovate. Understanding and harnessing these technological advances becomes crucial for the next generation of creative practitioners entering an AI-driven creative economy.
This course explores the profound impact of artificial intelligence on the creative industries, including film, design, advertising, and music. Students will gain extensive hands-on experience with cutting-edge generative AI tools across multiple creative domains - from text and image generation to AI video synthesis, audio creation, and generative web/app prototyping. By combining theory with extensive practical workshops and industry engagement, students will learn how these technologies are reshaping creative workflows and business models, preparing them to meet the evolving needs of the creative sector in the AI era.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. #### Explain core concepts of generative AI, including LLMs and diffusion models, in the context of creative industries.
2. #### Analyse and reflect on real-world cases of AI applications in film, design, advertising, and music.
3. #### Apply generative AI tools to create original textual, visual, or audio content relevant to creative projects.
4. #### Prototype a creative solution or digital product that incorporates AI features using accessible, no-code platforms, demonstrating practical application in a creative industry context.
5. #### Demonstrate ethical awareness and responsible use of AI, including transparent citation and acknowledgment of AI-generated content.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to the Art Market
courses.description:
The artworld is constructed through a network of individuals and institutions, all of which participate in con-tributing to the wider ecosystem of the global network and marketplace for art. The co-generative or mutu-ally constitutive nature between key players and institutions provides the context and rules for evaluating the aesthetic and economic value of art objects. In recent years, the art market has witnessed tremendous growth, and clusters of new galleries, global art fairs and auction houses have sprung up in cities within both developed and emerging economies, forming an ever-expanding network of art transitions, exhibi-tions, and causing an explosion of cultural activities amid various forms of urbanization.

This course aims to provide students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills on how to identify the dynamic roles and activities of key players and institutions in the art market. It begins with an introduction to the history of art market, patronage system and art market logic. The, various practical skills are covered, including art valuation methods, techniques of buying and selling art, and agreements and laws that govern art transactions. In addition to practical skills, this course also encourages students to critically evaluate the complex relationships between the economy, aesthetic values and social behaviors within the global market-place. Special focus will be on emerging technologies and platforms concerning the global online art market.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing this course, students will be able to:

• Identify the roles and activities of key players and institutions in the art market

• Explain and analyze the history of the art market, patronage system and art market logic

• Develop skills in art valuation, the buying and selling of art, creating agreements and understanding the laws that govern art transactions

• Acquire personal and social competencies in connecting with the art community and pursuing future careers

• Develop skills in critical analysis concerning the complex relationships between the economy, aesthetic values and social behaviors within the global marketplace

• Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by understudying emerging technologies and plat-forms concerning the global online art market

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Music, Culture and Outreach
courses.description:
It is of crucial significance for cultural practitioners and managers to develop a solid foundation and capability in understanding the nature of music from various perspectives, as well as possessing the competency in appreciating the aesthetic and artistic value of musical works for the sake of advocating, marketing, coordinating and managing various programmes, events and outreach in music. Through exploring a wide range of music literature from different historical periods in music, the course focuses on three main perspectives:

The first perspective focuses on listening and examining the major masterpieces in the history of music from Middle Ages to Modern, in which musical elements and characteristics of major forms and genres will be introduced and analysed. The second perspective is identified by the relationship of music to culture, in which the influence that cultural, social, political and religious events have exerted on music will be discussed. The third perspective focuses on experiencing and examining the approaches of music education in advocating music in the society. Through experiential learning, students will be able to develop basic knowledge and skills for applying the current theories and approaches in music education (e.g. play-based approach, Orff Schulwerk, Dalcroze, Kodaly) to outreach and education in the society.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Visual Arts Management
courses.description: This course leads students to study various modes and philosophies of visual arts management undertaken in different venues. Aesthetics and art criticisms are critical in directing art interpretation and presentation. Contemporary management of visual arts responds predominantly to the worldwide discussions on modernism as well as various post-modernist writings. In addition, it has to operate in accordance with the prescribed state policy. For this bilateral concern of art management, the course comprises two sections. The first section leads students to study the writings on aesthetics by critics from Plato to Foucault, whose arguments are still valid in inspiring many art exhibitions. The second section discusses the practical concerns and techniques in maximizing the social and economic impacts of art exhibitions and relevant events. Both sections discuss case studies taken from different parts of the world.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe different categories of visual arts in professional language; to define and explain the key terms in visual art literature; to appreciate and analyze art exhibitions with reference to intellectual debates on aesthetics; to describe and explain the art policies implemented in East Asia and the West; and to develop independent thinking on the operation and promotion of art organizations.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Performing Arts Management
courses.description: This course discusses the missions, administrations, and strategies of performing art organizations. Since the 1950s, performing art managers have realized the significance of efficient management in achieving popularity and sale. This course will go through the general topics as to how the performing art organizations are administered in national and legal terms; how they solicit funding; how they are operated in terms of ticketing and touring; and how they are strategically promoted for both branding and social benefits.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe the practical concerns of the performing art organizations in terms of their daily operation; to identify various sources of funding in support of performing arts; to evaluate the administration structure and strategies undertaken in different countries; and describe and explain the different policies implemented in East Asia and the West.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Film and Literature: Inter-Media Studies
courses.description: This course's objective is to acquaint students with the kindred relationships between film and literature as well as to help them develop a more critical awareness to appreciate these two media from a cultural studies perspective. It will cover the following topics: introduction to the art of film, the generic and mediumistic comparisons of film and literature: film and the novel or film and drama or the theatre, etc.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning Outcomes

Students are expected to develop interdisciplinary perspectives to understand and be critical of the following:

- Cultural production, circulation, and consumption are ideologically and economically linked.

- Community preservation and regeneration, cultural diversity, and cultural participation are important in the building of a better society.

Students are expected to develop the following skills and values:

- Ability in critically analyzing the diversity of values and interests in society

- Literacy in different forms of visual and verbal expression, understanding how meanings and affects are constructed in different media forms and genres

- Ability in drawing on a number of disciplinary origins within areas of the arts, humanities and social sciences to appreciate the richness and the usefulness of interdisciplinary approach

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Animals, Culture and Modern Society
courses.description:
(UGEC3481 is double-coded with CURE3003.)

How do we understand and connect to animal kingdom?
How do human-animal connections shape modern culture and society?
How do cultural studies and humanities expand our scope on animal and nature?

Culture is ordinary, in Raymond William’s saying, but the ordinariness is merely treated as a reflection of human everyday life. Although cultural studies has sustained concern on everyday life with mass production, consumerism, sexism, racism and postmodernism, the discipline always lags behind the concern of nature and animal species. As the issues of animal abuse, environmental protection, factory farming, animal protection policy and law-making, as well as media various portrayals being the hot topics of our (post)modern world, the study of animal with the perspective of cultural studies and other humanity disciplines can explore the possibilities of better human-animal relationship. This course is designed with an empathic concern of other-than-human animals. By exploring different issues of human and animals’ life, this course looks for a harmonious balance of nature and modern culture.

This course focuses on three areas, through which we can explore the different aspects of animal and cultural studies. These areas are:
A. Entering Jurassic Park – Remaking Animals in Leisure (Lecture A1-A4)
B. Attacking Godzilla – Representing Animals in Media (Lecture B1-B4)
C. Finding Nemo – Revitalizing Animals in the City (Lecture C1-C4)

Each area covers a set of animal issue discussion. Area A, apart from theorizing animal with cultural studies, tackles the basic animal issues: pet-nurturing, zoo-building, forest-sustaining and tourism. This is to provide a foundation for understanding animals with a critical reflection of everyday life.

Area B, set with the concern of media, discusses issues of animal representation in cartoon, cinema, literature and journalism. This is to read how animals would be represented and how this affects human understanding and related policy-making. A screening will be run after Lecture Area B. This is to provide an alternative understanding of animal representation in popular media.

Area C further deals with the matters of animal-city relationship in seeing how dogs and cats, cattle and swine, and fishes and dolphins are (mal)treated in the street, the farm and the sea respectively. This is to end the course with a leading thought of perfect balance of nature and modernity; and more queries of human-animal relationship will be raised for contemplation.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Cultural Studies
courses.description: What is gender and why does it matter? What are the significances and limitations of gender as an analytic category? How are dominant understandings and practices of gender constructed and contested in different cultural forms and social contexts? This course is divided into three sections. The first section introduces the basic vocabulary of gender studies and how gender intersects with other forms of differences. The second section explores gender through various cultural products and media (e.g. literature, film, video games, theatre, social activism, etc.) The final section examines key debates in relation to gender in specific social contexts. Upon completion of this course, students would understand basic theoretical concepts for gender analysis and key debates on gender as well as gain the ability to think critically about gender.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning outcomes

Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1) understand basic theoretical concepts for gender analysis and debates on gender

2) analyze how gender intersects with other forms of differences

3) use the key concepts and theories to analyze a specific cultural phenomenon from a gendered perspective

4) critically think about gender

courses.title: Special Topics: Public Humanities Workshop
courses.description: The specific topics of this course vary from year to year. Generally, the lecturer would introduce students to specific ideas and themes related to public humanities, and the lecturer would encourage and work with students to develop different projects to explore the concerned ideas and themes.
courses.learning_outcomes:

2) Students are expected to develop creative skills in art and design and gain capabilities to transform humanistic values into cultural projects that inspire community development in the society.
