(4)Ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious traditions especially those one does not belong.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Hong Kong Culture and Heritage
courses.description: This course introduces students to critical approaches and practices related to cultural heritage, with a focus on case studies from Hong Kong. It emphasizes the interdisciplinary nature of the field and encourages students to challenge and reflect on “Eurocentric” theories and practices of heritage. Structured thematically, the first part of the course covers current debates in both the theory and practice of cultural heritage, including issues such as definition, authenticity, ethics, tangible and intangible heritage, cultural rights, commodification, sustainability, and inclusiveness. The second part of the course uses case studies from Hong Kong to examine how certain sites or practices have been institutionalized and listed as local or international heritages. It also explores various models of defining and managing Hong Kong's cultural heritage. By the end of the course, students will be able to think beyond “Eurocentric” heritage concepts and practices, and be aware of the correlation between Hong Kong cultural heritage, identity, and community.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Understand the critical approaches to cultural heritage management.
2. Understand current debates on the Eurocentric approaches to cultural heritage
3. Demonstrate familiarity of a range of issues related to Hong Kong cultural heritage
4. Demonstrate written and oral skills in analysis and presentation of Hong Kong cultural heritage
5. Demonstrate ability to apply methods and theories of cultural heritage management

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Film and Independent Cinema
courses.description:
From the emergence of Hollywood's studio and star systems to the diversity of international cinema, including the rise of independent and avant-garde movements, and the expansion of cinema on online platforms, the study of cinema encompasses various facets, such as industry, artistic expression, and cultural and curatorial practices. This course situates cinema within extensive aesthetic, economic, and curatorial frameworks, offering students foundational knowledge in film analysis, film studies languages and concepts, the history of both mainstream and independent films, and the evolving technological, cultural, and generic significance of film. These often intersect with issues of cultural identity, representation, and power structures.
Additionally, the course addresses the curatorial aspects of film exhibitions and festivals in various venues, such as festivals, museums, archives, online platforms, and emerging virtual technologies. Students interested in cultural management and cultural studies in the context of film and independent cinema will gain the skills to analyze, curate, and critically engage with film, focusing on models, aesthetics, culture, and curatorial practices.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Understand major filmmaking movements, film analysis techniques, and key concepts and terminologies in film studies.
* Explain the history of both mainstream and independent films.
* Examine critical issues related to the evolving technological, cultural, and genre significance of film.
* Develop the skills and knowledge necessary to curate film exhibitions and festivals in various venues.
* Foster an attitude of innovation and creativity through discussions on the future of cinema and curatorial strategies in film.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Media Arts Management
courses.description: This course introduces a new genre in the art discipline that employs electronic and digital devices as the main medium of communication. The course contains three sessions. The first session explains the birth of this set of contemporary art practices in relation to the Dadaist movement of the early twentieth century that opened up new concepts for visual arts. This will be followed by a session that discusses the range of media now commonly adopted in the discipline, including video, photography, computer graphics, webpage, and the Internet. Different set of techniques are involved in these productions, and they often generate quite different social impacts that affect both the producers and the users. Students are instructed to understand both the technological and social aspects of these areas. The last session comprises a series of workshops that lead students to appreciate and comment on the most featured productions. Emphasis is placed on the angle to promote this new art type as a rising cultural sector in the society.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe and define the technical terms employed in the new media productions; to acquire the basic techniques involved in shooting, controlling sound effect, and designing for interactive visual experience; to identify the software and skills essential for creating different virtual experience; to recognize the economic aspects of using multi-media in cultural sectors; to analyze the social coverage and impacts of using the Internet for distribution; and to develop independent thinking about the cyber-culture and artificial identity.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Public and Community Art

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408

courses.description: Public art is considered as an important cultural asset of metropolitan cities, closely related to city images and development. Community art serves as a tool for community development, based on the understanding that expression, mastery and communication through the arts powerfully encode cultural values, thus bringing deeper meanings of experience, participation and involvement, sense of belonging to the general public and the community. This course aims to advance students’ understanding of public and community arts by embedding them in the theoretical discussions and critiques of cities and public spaces and practical experiences. It also imparts the knowledge and skills about managing public arts and actualizing community art programs, and discusses the way to support their development responding to the needs.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge acquisition, students are expected to understand how public and community arts emerged in the context of urban regeneration and community activist movements. Students are encouraged to critically analyze the meanings and social values of public art spaces. In terms of managerial concepts and skills, students will learn how public and community arts are supported by government policies, material resources, infrastructure and training. Students are expected to understand public art commission and reception, to master basic principles of utilizing public art as an urban design strategy, and to apply varying approaches to facilitating community art development, for example, advancing community art education, utilizing the cultural planning approach to assess community based cultural resources and the place-event approach to creating a sense of community attachment.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Design Your Exhibition – Curatorial Planning and Practice
courses.description:
“Curator” once referred to an expert in keeping collections and making exhibitions, but has been expanded to encompass a hybrid role in innovation and knowledge creation. Today, curators are active agents in social and cultural transformation, taking part in dynamic projects presented by museums, commercial galleries, non-profit art spaces, biennials, art fairs, and many disruptive platforms beyond the field of art that didn’t previously exist. Curators produce knowledge, engage their audience, spark innovation, and constantly challenge the role of “curator” beyond the confines of the status quo across varied institutional settings.

This course aims to provide students with hands-on experience in exhibition curation and engages students in a broad spectrum of real-world experiences and professional networking opportunities, aiming to prepare students for future curatorial projects/jobs. It covers topics such as idea conceptualization, proposal writing, pitching, budgeting, contracting, publication, exhibition design, installation and exhibition maintenance. By co-curating an exhibition in a non-profit art space in Hong Kong, students will take part in the various stages of exhibition making. With a focus on exhibition experience, audience engagement, and sociability, this course will train students in the role of being a curator and enable students to develop leadership skills and critically apply knowledge conducive to creative outcomes.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
1. Pre-requisite: CUMT2007 Curation in Arts and Culture or CURE2407 Curation in Arts and Culture
2. Not for students who have taken CUMT3005.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing the course, students will be able to:
• Explain the key roles of being a curator
• Develop skills in the various stages of exhibition making from a broad spectrum of real-world experience and professional networking opportunities
• Acquire personal and social competencies to work cooperatively in a team
• Develop critical analysis skills concerning exhibition experiences, audience engagement and sociability
• Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions in the ever-expanding field of curation

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Popular Music and Industry
courses.description: “Popular Music and Industry” is an interdisciplinary course that examines the complex relationship between popular music, culture, arts management, and the evolving music industry. Students will explore the historical development of popular music genres and styles, analyze the interplay between music and society, and evaluate the key stakeholders, business models, and technological transformations that have shaped the popular music landscape over time. Through a combination of international case studies, critical discussions, and hands-on research, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the popular music industry, from record labels and publishing to streaming platforms and live events. The course will also explore and assess the impact of globalization, cultural exchange, and emerging technologies on the future development of production, distribution, and consumption of popular music worldwide.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

* Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the historical development and evolution of popular music genres, styles, and trends over the past century.
* Analyze the complex interplay between popular music, culture, arts administration, and society, and how they influence and shape one another.
* Evaluate the key stakeholders, institutions, and business models that constitute the popular music industry, including record labels, music publishers, streaming platforms, and live events.
* Critically examine the role of technology, digital media, and social platforms in shaping the production, distribution, and consumption of popular music.
* Assess the impact of globalization, cultural exchange, and transnational flows on the global popularity, management, and commercialization of various popular music genres.
* Apply analytical and research skills to investigate and discuss contemporary issues and debates within the popular music industry, such as intellectual property rights, artist compensation and management, and the changing nature of music consumption in the global context.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Entrepreneurship in the Creative Industries
courses.description: The concept of “creative industry” was proposed by the Labor Party in the U.K. in 1997. It refers to the activities that are embedded in individuals’ creativities, talents and skills, which have the potential for employment opportunities and economic growth through the exploitation of intellectual properties. Creative industry has become a key area in contemporary cultural policies. This course introduces students to the basic knowledge of managing entrepreneurship, which is a key issue in the creative industries. It comprises three parts. The first part provides a general introduction. The second part discusses the nature of entrepreneurship in creative industries and demonstrates the entrepreneurial process, through which, creative ideas are generated, cultural diffusion is stimulated and innovation processes are carried out. It informs students of the key traits of the creative entrepreneurs and the business opportunities and models for entrepreneurship processes in the creative industries. In the third part, it explores the conducive policy conditions to support and encourage entrepreneurship in creative industries.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, a student will:
i) Have their understanding being deepened about creative industries and entrepreneurship
ii) Value and appreciate entrepreneurial spirits in the creative industries
iii) Develop sets of skills for entrepreneurial practices
iv) Understand the policy conditions for entrepreneurship and acquire consultation skills for the government

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Curating and Managing Arts Festival
courses.description: With a global growing interest in organizing grand scale arts and cultural activities to attract local and overseas audience, arts festivals have become popular urban cultural events for cultural development and for building the reputation of a city. Curating and managing cultural festival is subsequently an important area of studies in cultural management. Curating and managing arts festival is a complex process that requires creative programming, skillful execution and careful financial control. This course not only studies the mode of operations of various types of cultural festivals, including festivals of performing arts, visual arts, film, literary arts and community festive celebration, but also introduces to students the basic skills and knowledge of curating and managing arts festivals, with references to local and overseas examples.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Interpretation of Heritage
courses.description:
Cultural heritage is a dynamic and evolving concept that encompasses various interpretations rather than being a fixed notion. It includes a wide range of perspectives, from Eurocentric to post-colonial, with an increasing focus on living culture that intertwines global and local narratives. This field involves diverse interpretive lenses, public discourse, human rights issues, and a shift from mere observation to immersive experiences. The interpretations of cultural heritage are shaped by numerous stakeholders, including educators, public program participants, researchers, writers, designers, creatives, consultants, curators, scientists, and historians. In recent years, technological advancements have further enhanced the use of digital media and social networking in cultural heritage, fostering new connections between visitors and heritage. Consequently, the interpretation of cultural heritage remains dynamic and fluid, embracing a variety of approaches and philosophies.
This course aims to provide students with a broad knowledge of cultural heritage interpretations and the theoretical frameworks that offer different lenses and approaches for thinking about cultural heritage. It covers various types of cultural heritage, the role of storytelling in heritage interpretation, heritage as public discourse, identity issues, visitor engagement and education, tourism, community involvement, and ethical issues. Additionally, this course will examine how technology plays a role in engaging audiences and facilitating interpretations. By offering students diverse concepts of cultural heritage interpretations, they will gain a comprehensive understanding of current interpretive approaches, emerging trends, and innovations in the interpretation of heritage.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT3009 or CUMT4101 or CURE4411.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explore key approaches, philosophies, and theories of cultural heritage interpretation.
* Understand cultural heritage as an evolving concept, encompassing various types of heritage, the role of storytelling, public discourse, identity issues, visitor engagement, tourism, community involvement, and ethical considerations.
* Examine critical issues related to current interpretive approaches, emerging trends, and innovations in heritage interpretation.
* Develop skills to critically interpret cultural heritage and its relationship with technology.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing approaches to cultural heritage interpretation.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Inclusive Theatre and Development of Sustainability in Arts
courses.description:
The objectives of this course are to deepen students’ understanding of “inclusivity” within the performing arts, addressing the needs and experiences of people with physical and mental disabilities, neurodiverse individuals, older adults, ethnic minorities, people of diverse gender identities and sexual orientations, multilingual groups, low-income backgrounds, and other marginalised communities. Students will master the principles of “sustainable development” as applied to the arts ecosystem, constructing a comprehensive framework that integrates environmental concerns such as green production, social dimensions like equity and accessibility, and economic aspects involving viable operational models. The course will also develop students’ practical creative and production skills by guiding them to design a theatre or arts project that upholds both “accessibility” and “low-carbon/circular” principles, including all practical aspects such as budgeting, venue selection, promotion, risk management, and evaluation. Furthermore, students will establish ethical and collaborative working methods, learning to co-create with communities while avoiding tokenistic representations and exploitative participation, especially within the context of Hong Kong. Finally, students will enhance their abilities in critical evaluation, assessing the effectiveness of inclusivity and sustainability using both qualitative and quantitative approaches, and formulating strategies for ongoing improvement.

The core themes of the course encompass a range of essential concepts. Firstly, “inclusive aesthetics” involves raising accessibility from merely a support measure to a deliberate creative language and aesthetic decision. Secondly, the principle of “accessibility by design” focuses on universal design practices, including relaxed performances, audio description, subtitles or sign language, and ensuring accessible front-of-house and information design. The third theme, “sustainable production”, addresses environmentally responsible approaches such as material recycling, establishing low-carbon stage setups, green procurement processes, waste reduction initiatives, efficient touring logistics, and energy management. The course also explores Hong Kong’s cultural and policy context, considering aspects like funding systems, venue regulations, audience profiles, educational linkages, social welfare partnerships, and community networks. Finally, themes of ethics, power, and representation are central, guiding students through issues of co-authorship, obtaining consent for data and image use, maintaining creative safety, and respecting care and boundaries within collaborative settings.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: CURE2412 Performing Arts Management or CUMT3002 Performing Arts Management or CURE3408 Curating and Managing Arts Festival or CUMT3008 Curating and Managing Arts Festival
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Learn to create the inclusion theatre for different purposes, which are the theatre made by the disabled, the theatre for the disabled and the concept of promoting fairness and equality [Introduction to create the inclusion theatre].
2. Learn to create comprehensive accessibility plans for performances, including elements such as subtitling, audio description, sign language interpretation, relaxation sessions, tactile tours, accessible front-of-house routes, and sensitive information alerts. Examine potential barriers throughout the ‘Audience Journey’—from information access and ticketing to arrival, seating, viewing, and departure [Competence (Inclusion)].
3. Implement simplified carbon accounting for stage productions, focusing on four key sources: materials, transport, energy, and waste. Design circular scenography by developing strategies for renting, recycling, repurposing, and modularising sets and costumes [The Idea of Sustainability].
4. Integrate inclusivity and sustainability into an executable team project proposal, covering aspects such as creative concept, target audience, collaboration methods, timeline, budget, staffing, risk management, and evaluation metrics [Implementation Capability].
5. Design foundational assessments using surveys, interviews, observations, and focus groups. Present outcomes and impacts through frameworks such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) or the theory of change [Research and Evaluation Competence].
6. Facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration and ensure clear communication with social welfare organisations, arts administrators, front-of-house teams, technical crews, and accessibility consultants [Communication and Collaboration].

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Museum Studies
courses.description:
Museums have multiple roles in a society. They are academic institutes and public arenas for education. In the broad term, they represent national culture and communal heritage. This course leads students to understand museum exhibitions and management within social contexts. The lectures respond to the following issues:
1. What are the functions and achievements of museum activities?
2. In what ways can we understand and learn from an exhibition? What are the essential elements of museum catalogues and cultural writing?
3. How do museum workers balance both marketing and social needs?
4. In what ways can we participate in the operation of a museum?
The course draws discussions from both the perspectives of museum workers and visitors. Some current issues concerning the roles of museums are also covered.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT3108 or ANTH4720 or HIST5514

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Global Cultural Theories
courses.description:
Departing from the dominant canon of critical theory, this course aims to introduce students to a wider, more diverse range of theoretical texts and frameworks by marginalized voices and from peripheral locations.
This course seeks to decolonize theory by multiplying the sites of intellectual and critical inquiry. Instead of treating Benjamin, Adorno, Hall, and Grossberg as representative of the corpus of theory, it engages with prevailing discussions in Postcolonial Studies, Modernity/Coloniality, and Black Studies. It moves beyond the call for ‘de-Westernization’ by looking at theoretical texts and frameworks produced in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The course concludes by exploring work about indigeneity, memory, and environmentalism.
The course is designed for advanced undergraduates with familiarity in critical approaches to literature, cinema, art, and media. Classes will grapple with the following questions: What qualifies as theory? Is theory necessarily abstract? What is the relationship of theory to particularity and difference? How can theory be made more attune to its contexts of production, dissemination, and application? How can film and visual art offer sources for theorizing? How might theoretical frameworks respond more significantly to social, economic, and environmental conditions from the restructuring of the capitalist system, expansion of media networks, dissolution of national borders, and deterioration of the climate crisis?
courses.learning_outcomes:
The objectives are:

1. To become acquainted with theoretical texts and frameworks in Cultural Studies by marginalized voices from different peripheral social and geographic contexts
2. To apply theory to analyze the articulation of race, gender, memory, and nature in literature, cinema, art, and media
3. To formulate, develop, write, and revise an original critical essay using global cultural theories

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Graduation Thesis
courses.description: This course provides an opportunity for students to undertake supervised study on a selected topic of interest. Students will be led to examine aspects of the selected topic, conduct a critical literature review and a systematic investigation of the topic they have chosen. Students are required to regularly discuss with the teacher concrete findings in their research and submit written progress reports as scheduled by the teacher and a complete project report at the end of the term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Apply theory critically to analyse cultural texts they interested.
2. Use a self-reflective approach to devising and developing an academic paper.
3. Reflectively evaluate their learning and personal planning processes.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: World Cinema in East Asia: Theory and Practice
courses.description:
The concept of world cinema emerged in the late 1980s during a period of transformation within the film industry, driven by advancements in technology, shifts in capital and changes in geopolitics. This course focuses on key issues such as representation, language and the film industry, while also examining how new technologies and global networks of distribution and screening have reshaped the production, circulation, and aesthetics of films.
The course places particular emphasis on Japanese, Chinese and Korean cinemas. Students will engage with theoretical frameworks informed by existing research from diverse disciplines, including the humanities, film and media studies, and cultural studies. By the end of the course, students will be well equipped to approach world cinema in two ways: theoretically, through critiques of representation and ideology, and practically, through inquiries into the cultural industry of film.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* **Trace and r****ecognise** the historical and theoretical development of a wide range of Asian films
* **Understand and analysis** the style, aesthetic and cinematic articulation of selected films.
* **Identify** **and em****ploy** a range of theoretical tools to engage with important discourses and debates on the development of Asian Cinema.
* **Identify and e****mploy** a range of theoretical tools to interrogate the impact of cultural policy, industries and film festivals to the transnational production, circulation and reception of Asian films.
* **Critically reflect on and theorise** the emerging trends of Asian cinema in theory and in practice.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Critical Approaches to Pornography
courses.description:
The course will offer an introduction to critical views on pornography, which is defined as sexually explicit media within different cinematic traditions and digital screen cultures. The aim of the course is to show that pornography is a not a unified screen culture but consists of varied representations within cultural contexts. The course will teach students how to analyze these representations and how to take into account their cultural histories.

The course will take a Cultural Studies approach and examine within specific cultural environments and include the positions of anti-porn and pro-porn activists. Therefore students will get an overview of diverging perspectives while being encouraged to consider their own values and critical responses. Students will be asked to respond to theories and audio-visual examples, while actively partaking in debates about pornography and its impact on religion, gender, sexuality, health, labor and economy. Finally, the course will pay special importance to how contemporary sexually explicit media are impacting new user groups such young adult netizens, female consumers, disabled people, as well as ethnic and sexual minorities.

Students will carry out a major assignment while learning how to apply ethnographic research methods to analyze representations of the body and sexuality within screen cultures. In this assignment, they will focus on a media environment/platform and a sexual culture of their choice to find out how culture is being redefined and visualized by media users. Two workshops will be organized in the media lab in order to train the students in different methods and perspectives on digital ethnography

Language of instruction: Classes and assignments will be carried out in the English language and students’ active participation in both lectures and tutorials will be required. Students can carry out ethnographic fieldwork in Cantonese or any language of your choice, but need to present the results in English.

Learning Activities: Students are required to attend a 3-hour class each week. The course combines theoretical lectures with the viewing of films and media examples. There will also be tutorial sessions each week based on the lectures and on the weekly readings. All students are required to post weekly reflections on Blackboard and to participate in discussions. In addition to the weekly readings and reflections, students will conduct research and planning for their assessments and oral presentations independently and in groups.

Please be advised that this course will involve some screenings and discussions of sexually explicit materials and category III films. Therefore, students under 18 years-old are advised not to take this course.
courses.component:
Field Studies/Field-trip
Laboratory
Lecture
Interactive Tutorial
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of the course, the students will be able to:

1. Analyze representations of sexuality within film aesthetics and screen cultures.

2. Understand the diversity of screen cultures in how they represent sexuality and sexually explicit media.

3. Understand contemporary debates about pornography and take a critical position.

4. Understand the unique position and cultural heritage of Hong Kong within East-Asian screen cultures.

5. Understand the relationship between sexual representations and social, religious or political tensions within cultural environments.

6. Apply ethnographic methods to analyze urban sexualities and online screen cultures.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Film Classics: Aesthetics and Politics
courses.description: This course aims at introducing some of the major film classics from America (Hollywood), Europe (France and Italy), Japan, and China produced from the earliest era to circa 1960. They will be viewed and studied in a cultural and historical context, together with detailed analysis of their form and content in order to understand their "canonical" status. Basic film theories - especially those dealing with film genres and film "auteurs" - will also be used.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Workshop in Creative Content
courses.description: Through workshops, this course aims to cultivate students' creative thinking and abilities of artistic expression. It leads students to explore various art forms, such as graphics, sound, non-fiction narrative, drama, experimental film, and cross/inter-disciplinary arts, etc. Specific projects are planned and executed around particular themes through primarily teacher-student consultations and discussions supplemented by lectures. It helps students grasp creative skills to express their opinions and emotions effectively using audiovisual elements. This advanced practical course requires students to have completed the foundational course CURE2066 Visual Design Foundation in advance.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Develop the creative and technical skills necessary to express students' opinions.
2. Enhance the ability to appreciate and think critically about various forms of artistic works while developing the critical, analytical, and editing skills necessary to evaluate works in progress, both in the student's own projects and those of their peers.
3. Improve students' communication and teamwork skills.
4. Learn how to showcase works and develop the ability to engage in dialogues with society.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Arts, Propaganda and Social Action
courses.description: The course studies the history, theories and techniques of organizing cultural activities for social and political causes. It investigates the relationship between cultural expressions and the infrastructure of power, and the application of arts and culture for social, political actions, covering such major movements from the avant-garde of the 19th Century, the USSR and the Chinese propaganda movements, to the arts for civil right movements since 1960s. Case studies of similar movements in Hong Kong will also be included. The final part of the course will introduce to students the operational and managerial skill required for organizing such cultural activities.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. A historical understanding of the use of arts as instrument for political propaganda and for actions for social improvement
2. An understanding of the various methods techniques applied in utilizing arts for social activism
3. Ability to undertake critical review of social actions, both in terms of techniques, strategy and communication.
4. An understanding of the ethical and cultural sensibility required for conducting community arts activities as social actions.

1. 從歷史發展的角度，了解藝術作為政治宣傳和社會改良運動的工具，被運用的情況；
2. 掌握在社會行動中，藝術運用的多種方法和技巧；
3. 能夠對社會行動，進行批判性評論，包括技巧、策略和溝通等方面。
4. 理解組織社區藝術活動時所要求具備的在倫理和文化上的敏感性。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Digital Imaging, Book Production and Contemporary Arts
courses.description:
This course will teach the conceptual foundations and implement the use of practices of digital imaging and book production okmaking within contemporary arts. The course will also teach aspects of contemporary art and photography as a documentary and conceptual medium. It will focus on digital imaging’s ability to enhance existing literature, and reproduce or manipulate pre-existing images. Students will be expected to equally apply digital imaging applications in a technically adept and creative manner with an eye towards given art historical movements and examples such as Dada and Surrealism.

The course will be based on software instruction, as well as use of digital scanning, digital photography and video productions . Assignments will include (but not be limited to) desktop publishing for the making of artist books, catalogues “zines” (inexpensive DIY magazines) and e-books that are consumed on various digital media format such websites, mobile phones and i-pad tablets.
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of the course students will be able to:

1. Understand and apply software applications such as Adobe Photoshop and Dobe InDesign for creative and commercial design projects.

2. Have a working knowledge of contemporary art as it relates to digital imaging, photography and book making.

3. Develop an individualized aesthetic in book making based on the potential of digital imaging.

4. Apply an understanding of cyberculture and digital media publishing as it applies to literary and audio-visual production and distribution.

成功完成本科的學生將會：

1. 理解和應用軟件程式，並用於創意和商業設計項目之中，例如Adobe Photoshop和Dobe InDesign
2. 具備有效的當代藝術知識，涉及數碼成像、攝影和編輯
3. 基於數碼成像的潛力，發展出個人在書籍製作上的審美趣味
4. 應用對賽博文化和數碼媒體出版的理解於文學、視聽製作和出版之上

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Documentary Studies: Theories and Practices
courses.description: The course explores the history and basic theory of documentary film. General concepts, aesthetics, ethics and different forms of documentary will be introduced as well. The aim of it is to help students develop a critical understanding and appreciation of documentary through lecture, screening, practical workshop and experience of creating a film. It also helps them to know how to discover and represent the cultural phenomenon in daily life by using visual method. Students are expected to finish their short documentary films at the end of the semester.
courses.learning_outcomes:
To equip students with general knowledge of the concepts and the history of documentary film.

• To analyze the close connection between history, culture, and cinema in documentary film.

• Students will understand how to conceive, shoot and edit a documentary.

• To use digital media as a tool in research and as a method of presenting research outcomes.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Summer Internship
courses.description: Process of cultural production and cultural practices at various levels are essential to the training of cultural sensitivity and analysis in cultural studies. This course aims to provide students with on-site experience of cultural production and practices for their reflection and integration of cultural theories and concepts they learnt in regular classes. Students will be introduced to a range of cultural institutions and culture-related non-governmental organizations for a placement of eight weeks between May to July during summer. Students will be asked to attend several sessions of orientations and evaluation before and during their placement.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Objectives:
Provide learning and practicing opportunities for students

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: AI, Arts and Technology
courses.description: What is the big deal about computational technologies for the arts? This course explores the evolution, current state, and future implications of artificial intelligence (AI) in art and media. This course provides an overview of the history of AI and computation from Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Besides concepts, students will explore the theories of art and technology through field trips and practices. Although history and critique are central to this course, students will also gain some hands-on experience in applications of AI in art. This course includes lectures, projects, and critical discussions. At the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate the inevitable integration of AI in creative workflows and its implications for the future of art, and articulate the critical issues and ethical implications of AI on creative arts.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Objectives**:

* *At the end of the course, the students should be able to**:

- Name the milestones and explain the historical development of AI from its inception to the current state.

- Assess the quality of Generative AI’s output in texts and images; categorize its weakness and strength and its impact on the creative process.

- Demonstrate awareness of the main ethical, legal, and environmental challenges posed by AI technologies by identifying arising issues and write critically about their societal impact.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chan School of Buddhism
courses.description: The Chan movement has been described by Hu Shih as a reformation or revolution in Buddhism and by Suzuki as a movement in which the Chinese mind completely asserted itself, in a sense, in opposition to the Indian mind. This course examines the Chan movement from a historical perspective. Attention will also be paid to the study of basic scriptures of the Chan School of Buddhism.
courses.learning_outcomes: We shall pay more attention to some most important figures and special features of Chan Buddhism within the framework of Buddhism. We will also explore the interaction between Chan Buddhism and Chinese. Throughout the course, students will be asked to critically analyze the rhetoric of modern scholarship on Chan/Zen so that they will understand Chan Buddhism in a broad perspective.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Selected Taoist Classics
courses.description: This course consists of reading of the classical literature of Taoism formulated in its early phase of development. Students are trained to understand Taoism through original textual reading. Selections include the T'ai-ping ching, the Pao-p'u tzu, the Chen-kao, and the Laotzu Hsiang-erh chu.
courses.learning_outcomes: To be able to understand religion in its historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally and locally and to analyze how contemporary religious expressions shape and are shaped by global and local cultural, social, and political trends.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Senior Seminar
courses.description: This course is to be taken by senior students who are required to write, under guidance and supervision, a thesis with the aim of integrating various areas of studies in theology and religion. Students will be evaluated on the ability to reflect upon major theological and religious issues.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topics in Religion, Culture and Heritage
courses.description:
An opportunity for guided research and study of selected topics, such as: methodological approaches to the study of religion, theories of religion, folk religion, festivals, religion in transition in contemporary society, the Mother goddess, religion as salvation, ritual and sacrifice. The Special Topics will also be covering in any other topics related to Special Topics in Religion, Culture and Heritage.

Students are allowed to take this course not more than twice, and gain the units each time they pass the course.

To be able to engage in a critical analysis of religions by the methods of the humanities and social sciences including textual and historical analysis, philosophical and hermeneutical studies, and social and cultural analysis.

Ability to gather, organize, deploy, synthesize and evaluate different types of evidence and information.

Self-critical awareness of presuppositions and recognition that statements should be tested, that evidence and arguments are subject to assessment, that the interpreter’s role demands critical evaluation.

courses.title: Special Topics in Religion, Society and Contemporary Issues
courses.description:
An opportunity for guided research and study of selected topics, such as: methodological approaches to the study of religion, theories of religion, folk religion, festivals, religion in transition in contemporary society, the Mother goddess, religion as salvation, ritual and sacrifice. Self-critical awareness of presuppositions and recognition that statements should be tested, that evidence and arguments are subject to assessment, that the interpreter’s role demands critical evaluation.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Internship
courses.description: Internship is a capstone, experiential learning course. This course aims to facilitate students to develop hands on experience in learning how to integrate academic concepts in Religious Studies with everyday circumstances. The course requires students to complete 150 hours of work experience within 8-10 weeks and a written essay.
courses.learning_outcomes:
As representatives of the Department, students are expected to behave with dedication professional integrity.

Learning outcomes:

1. Knowledge Outcomes

Students will be able to understand how academic training both informs, and is informed by practice.

1. Skills Outcomes

Students will be able to develop their communication and presentational (oral and written) skills as well as analytical and problem solving ability.

1. Attitude Outcomes

Students will be able to develop their awareness of plurality within religious traditions and multi-faceted complexity of religions.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Integrated Studies in Cultural Management
courses.description: This course is continuation of CUMT1001, Introduction to Cultural Management, and looks at cultural management from the macro perspective. Successful culture managers work to maintain healthy balance between culture and its relevant fields of interests, which sometimes could turn harmful or beneficial to the growth and development of the corresponding cultural area. The first session discusses the mutual dependence between culture and various areas, which include laws, economy, community, national interests, and art practitioners. In practice, cultural managers usually have to conform to the values and ethnics of the corresponding countries. For that reason, the second session will look at the approach taken in a few remarkable examples, which Taiwan, China, Singapore, South Korea, U.K., and the U.S.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain different national and social concerns for preserving culture; to identify the legal and ethnic issues relevant to cultural productions; to identify marketing strategies in cultural promotion; to evaluate the measures for maximizing the input of art practitioners; and to describe the various successful cultural schemes implemented in overseas countries.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Culture-led City Development
courses.description: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the culture-led city development phenomenon and equip them with the protocols for execution and practice. It comprises three blocks: Block 1 unfolds an overall picture of the phenomenon, introduces the related concepts, displays the disciplinary foundation of this topic, traces its history, and discusses the rationales and developing tendency. Block 2 studies the urban sociological and economic approaches employed in developing the theoretical foundation, highlighting a transition in capitalist production mode and urban governance upheld by public-private partnership modes. Criticisms are also presented to complete a dialectic mindset of this phenomenon. With a strong practical dimension, Block 3 teaches students various methods to make consultancy and policy recommendations for culture-led urban development projects. A variety of practices that constitute the culture-led strategy are discussed, such as how to plan for a creative city and cultural facilities, how to boost creative industries and develop cultural quarters and creative clusters, as well as how to revitalize historic quarters.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are introduced to the basic concept of the culture-led urban development phenomenon, recognizing related concepts, understanding its history, and developing tendencies in the world. Then, they can gain a deep theoretical understanding of the origins of these practices in a capitalist political economic transition, the corresponding urban policies, and the urban governance modes. Moreover, students can learn how to conduct policy analysis and apply urban planning and design principles to provide consultancy for culture-led city development projects. The final products of group projects shall consist of policy recommendations and project consultancies for the Hong Kong government or other private sector developers.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Heritage and Modern Applications
courses.description:
Cultural heritage is not confined to the past but is continuously carried forward into the present and future through various modern applications. These applications address current societal concerns, needs, and the ever-changing culture both locally and globally. The relevance of cultural heritage is influenced by complex power structures, including its presentation and representation in contexts such as postcolonialism, racial dynamics, gender, intergenerational equity, disparities in access to technology, marginalization, and the tension between localism and globalization. Additionally, the modern application of cultural heritage is shaped by evolving economic structures and technological advancements. Heritage is increasingly utilized by creative industries, with its assets digitized, interpreted, and experienced through advanced technologies such as AI and VR. Ensuring the continued relevance of cultural heritage has become a critical issue.
This course aims to provide students with an understanding of cultural heritage and its diverse modern applications, along with the critical concepts that shape our perception of its relevance today. It addresses issues concerning cultural heritage and its relationship with changing urban demographics, climate change, intergenerational equity, and the application of technologies for future alternatives. Additionally, the course explores cultural heritage as an economic generator, its role in performance, sports, and games, and its adoption in personalized tours and emerging cultural industries. Through a variety of concepts and case studies, students will gain multiple perspectives on current practices and reflect on the vast potential of cultural heritage in contemporary times.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students would be able to:

* Explore key examples of cultural heritage and its diverse modern applications, along with the critical concepts that shape our perception of its relevance today.
* Understand the modern applications of cultural heritage.
* Explain cases where cultural heritage acts as an economic generator.
* Reflect on broader critical issues surrounding the modern applications of cultural heritage, including but not limited to postcolonialism, racial dynamics, and other related topics.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing applications and projecting future directions in cultural heritage.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Digital Humanities and Data Visualization in Heritage Management
courses.description: Digital technologies have fundamentally altered the condition of heritage management, presenting not only opportunities but also complex conceptual and ethical challenges. This advanced seminar explores how digital technologies profoundly transform the ways we create, manage, interpret, and preserve our cultural heritage. We will interrogate the digital age as a cultural moment and a new epistemological space defined by its own distinct affordances, anxieties, and philosophical challenges. This course will equip students to not only use digital tools, but to think critically about their impact on the fabric and fabrication of cultural memory and heritage practice. By engaging with theorists, artists, and practitioners, we will question what heritage means when it is rendered as data, experience it through immersion, and subject it to the logics of artificial intelligence and network culture. Our readings and discussions are organized around these pressing questions, grounding theoretical concerns in practical case studies from Hong Kong and beyond.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* Demonstrate a critical understanding of the core theories, debates, and ethical challenges in digital art history and heritage.
* Analyze how digital technologies and archives reshape our relationship to culture, memory, and the past.
* Apply key digital humanities concepts, such as affordance, immediacy, enclosure, and spatial analysis to interpret digital artworks and case studies.
* Evaluate the social, political, and planetary implications of using digital tools in galleries, libraries, archives, and museums.
* Create a critically self-aware digital storytelling project that reflects on the practice of curating heritage online.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Advanced Museum Studies
courses.description:
This course picks up topics, which cannot be fully covered in CUMT4007 Museum Studies, but are essential for students pursuing careers in the area of museum and exhibition planning. This course is an advanced version, because it will touch on debated issues regarding museums. It focuses on installation, display, and site management. The purposes of the course may be summarized as follows:
1. What are the various display methods in museums? What are the concerns involved in selecting the ‘right’ ones?
2. How are museum workers (non-curatorial) trained?
3. What are the essential facilities a museum is expected to have? Why?
4. What is the role of museum in the contemporary arts, which is the area of debate regarding its significance and curatorship?

The course develops students’ awareness towards global developments in world-class museums, so that they are equipped with skills and knowledge necessary for long-term competition in museums or other cultural institutions.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
1. Pre-requisite(s): CUMT3108 Museum Studies or CURE3508 Museum Studies
2. Not for students who have taken CUMT4008.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. Analyze exhibition display methods and theories.

2. Think critically about display and social concerns.

3. Clarify the roles and potentials of museum workers.

4. Get prepared for career related to management of museums and cultural industries.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topics in Heritage Management
courses.description:
Cultural institutions such as museums, archives, and cultural centers play a critical role in the preservation, interpretation, and dissemination of heritage. Through diverse programs, place-making projects, and cultural policies, these institutions preserve and represent cultural memory, sustain community identity and continuity, and emphasize the importance of community involvement and participatory approaches. They ensure that both tangible and intangible heritage are accessible to the public and future generations. Additionally, they intersect with contemporary issues such as the impact of globalization, tourism, the role of policy-making and advocacy in heritage protection, and the influence of the digital age on cultural heritage.
This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in managing cultural heritage, with a particular emphasis on intangible heritage, which includes oral histories, performative rituals, social practices, and craftsmanship. Students will engage with diverse topics, exploring how the principles and practices of heritage management inform a variety of theories and approaches, such as cultural relativism, ethnocentrism, and post-colonial theory. By focusing on a chosen area of cultural heritage or a particular field of heritage theory, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on the challenges and opportunities presented by historical and current phenomena and to participate in projects with the potential to impact individuals and societies.

* Explain key historical and contemporary examples of cultural heritage projects, relating them to broader local and global contexts.
* Examine critical issues concerning the ways different methods of preservation, interpretation, and dissemination of heritage adopted by cultural institutions.
* Develop skills to critically analyze intangible heritage, including oral histories, performative rituals, social practices, and craftsmanship.
* Acquire personal and social competencies related to various forms of culture and become an active agent in managing cultural heritage.
* Foster an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing methods of preservation, interpretation, and dissemination of heritage.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topics in Curation
courses.description:
Curating in art and culture involves selecting and organizing artworks, cultural artifacts, practices, and narratives to create a cohesive exhibition that conveys a specific theme. This requires a deep understanding of the artists' intentions, the works' context, and diverse cultural expressions, as well as a commitment to preserving heritage and promoting dialogue. Curators play a crucial role in ensuring representation, authenticity, and inclusivity in the audience's experience. In recent years, the concept of curating has extended to social media, where it involves strategically choosing and presenting content to engage a digital audience. This includes managing visuals, texts, and interactive elements to create a compelling online presence. The term "curating," once limited to museums, now applies broadly, reflecting the growing importance of thoughtful content curation in effectively engaging and informing diverse audiences across various platforms.
This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in curation. Students will engage with diverse topics, exploring how various platforms offer unique opportunities for curators to select, organize, manage, and create artworks, artifacts, content, and knowledge. By covering various curatorial strategies in the ever-expanding field of knowledge production, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on current phenomena and curate projects that have the potential to impact individuals and societies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explain key historical and contemporary examples of curatorial practices and relate them to a broader local and global context.
* Examine critical issues concerning how different curatorial models impact knowledge production.
* Develop skills and gain hands-on experience in curatorial practices through field trips and participation in arts and culture, including curating cultural events in the community, such as festivals and exhibitions.
* Acquire personal and social competencies related to curation, and act as active agents in curating creative projects.
* Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing curatorial practices.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topics in Cultural Institutions
courses.description:
Cultural institutions are organizations that preserve, promote, and disseminate culture, knowledge, and heritage. These institutions can take various forms, ranging from museums, libraries, archives, and galleries to virtual and tech-based platforms. The evolution of cultural institutions reflects broader changes in cultural management models and organizational modes, influenced by ever-changing technology and societal shifts. From traditional museums, libraries, and archives to innovative digital and participatory models, cultural institutions are increasingly leveraging diverse approaches to enhance accessibility, engagement, and cultural impact.
This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in managing cultural institutions. Students will engage with diverse topics, exploring how various models and organizational modes within different types of cultural institutions inform a variety of theories and practices. By focusing on a chosen institutional form or specific field of cultural institutions, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on current phenomena and participate in projects that have the potential to impact individuals and societies.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topic in Creative Industries
courses.description:
In recent years, the rapid development of cultural and creative industries has transformed the way cultural products are created, produced and distributed. These industries, from theater and fashion to social media and game design, highlight how contemporary societies use intellectual and creative approaches to gain economic and symbolic competitiveness. Alongside technological innovations, the creative sector also plays a significant role in driving global economic transformation, offering government agencies and entrepreneurs new strategies to produce creative experiences not anticipated in the past.

This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in cultural and creative industries. Students will engage with a diverse range of topics, exploring how various sectors within these industries inform a variety of theories and practices. By covering multiple creative and entrepreneurial strategies in the ever-expanding field of cultural and creative industries, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on the current phenomenon and create projects that have the potential to impact individuals and societies.
